video_title: Up in the Garden and Down in the Dirt by Kate Messner - Children's Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: A child and Nana get the garden ready in spring. They clear away old plants, spread compost, and plant seeds. Under the soil, earthworms, insects, and pill bugs are busy too. Soon carrots, peas, tomatoes, and other plants grow. Bees and wasps visit the blossoms, while worms tunnel below. Rain fills the soil, and the roots drink the water. In summer, the child and Nana eat vegetables and pick cucumbers, zucchini, and bugs from the plants. At night, bats and skunks help in the garden. When autumn comes, pumpkins and sunflowers appear, and everyone gathers food before the cold. Ants store food, while beetles and worms hide underground. Frost arrives, and the garden becomes quiet. Under the snow, the plants and tiny animals rest and wait for warm sunshine, blossoms, and new sprouts to return.

In spring, a child visits the garden with Nana and wonders what is happening under the dirt. Nana explains that earthworms and insects are digging, building, and helping the soil. Together, they clean the garden, plant seeds, and give them water. The garden grows through summer. Carrots sprout, peas bloom, bees gather pollen, and many animals find food. The child enjoys warm tomatoes and helps harvest cucumbers and zucchini. At night, bats and skunks search for food. A praying mantis, a snake, spiders, birds, ladybugs, and other creatures also live in the garden. In autumn, pumpkins turn orange, leaves fall, and the family gathers food for the cold days. Frost covers the leaves. The people spread blankets over the garden, while ants, beetles, and earthworms hide below. Soon snow covers everything, and the sleeping garden waits for spring.

The story follows a garden from spring to winter. At first, the child wants to plant, but Nana says the soil must dry and warm. They remove weeds, add compost, make rows, and plant seeds. Below them, pill bugs, worms, and other insects work in the dirt. During summer, plants grow and flowers open. Bees visit, ladybugs eat aphids, roots drink rain, and many animals hunt for food. The child and Nana eat beans and tomatoes and gather vegetables. In the evening, bats fly and skunks dig. Later, pumpkins grow, sunflowers bow, and a spider spins a web. When the wind turns cool, the family harvests the garden and shares with neighbors. Frost comes, and the people cover the garden for winter. Ants, beetles, and worms settle underground. Even though the garden looks still beneath snow, life remains there, waiting for sunshine and spring growth.

video_title: The Rabbit Listened | Feelings and Kindness Story

summaries.summary: One day, Taylor built something new, special, and amazing. Taylor felt proud, but suddenly everything came crashing down. The chicken came first and said it was a shame. The chicken wanted Taylor to talk, but Taylor did not want to talk. Then the bear came and wanted Taylor to shout. Taylor did not want to shout either. Taylor did not want to do anything with them, so they all left. Then the rabbit came close and sat quietly with Taylor. Taylor asked the rabbit to stay. The rabbit listened while Taylor talked, shouted, remembered, laughed, and made plans. The rabbit stayed while Taylor planned to build again.

The hyena wanted to laugh, the ostrich wanted to hide, the kangaroo wanted to throw everything away, and the snake wanted to knock down something else. Taylor did not want to do any of those things. Soon, the animals left, and Taylor was alone. A rabbit quietly moved closer. Taylor asked it to stay. The rabbit listened to every feeling and every plan. At last, Taylor planned to build again.

Taylor asked, “Please stay with me.” The rabbit stayed and listened. It listened when Taylor talked, shouted, remembered, laughed, and made plans to hide or throw things away. The rabbit never left. Bald eagle places mistletoe, and snowy owl helps put it over the doors. Fox lights lanterns so the skaters can see. Hare wears snowshoes and makes hot Tundra tea. Polar bear cheers when penguins arrive for the tree-trimming party. The animals try to hang the star, but it is too hard. Narwhal helps by flinging the star from far away. Everyone watches the Northern Lights add holiday magic. Then the penguins go home to Antarctica. The Arctic friends send Christmas wishes across the icebergs, saying, “Merry Christmas!”

video_title: 🐵 Grumpy Monkey

summaries.summary: One wonderful day, Jim the chimpanzee woke up and felt that everything was wrong. The sky was too blue, the sun was too bright, and the bananas were too sweet. Norman, Mirabeau, the lemur, and Snake each noticed that Jim looked grumpy. They told him about his hunched body, bunched eyebrows, frown, and unhappy face. Jim tried to smile, but he still did not feel happy. The birds, monkeys, zebras, peacocks, and others invited him to sing, swing, roll, stroll, play, hug, laugh, nap, eat, jump, and dance. Jim did not want to do any of those things. He shouted and stormed away. Then Jim saw Norman looking grumpy too. Norman had hurt himself, but said he would probably feel better soon. Jim said he was still grumpy, but he would probably feel better soon too. Norman agreed that it was a wonderful day to be grumpy, and Jim felt a little better.

Jim the chimpanzee began a wonderful day feeling grumpy. He thought the bright sun, blue sky, and sweet bananas were all wrong. His friends saw that his body, eyebrows, and frown looked grumpy, even though Jim said he was not grumpy. After Jim tripped over Snake, everyone tried to help him feel better. They invited him to sing, swing, roll, stroll, lie in the grass, stomp, splash, hug, laugh, nap, eat, jump, and dance. Jim did not feel like doing anything. At last, he beat his chest, shouted that he was not grumpy, and stormed away. Jim then felt sorry for shouting at everyone and for himself. He admitted that he was grumpy. Soon he found Norman, who was also slumped and frowning because he hurt himself. Norman said he would feel better soon. Jim said he would too, but for now he needed to be grumpy. Then he felt a little better.

Jim woke up and could not enjoy the day. Everything seemed wrong to him: the light was too bright, the sky was too blue, and the bananas were too sweet. His friends tried to understand. Norman, Mirabeau, the lemur, and Snake pointed out that Jim stood hunched, had bunched eyebrows, and wore a frown. Jim smiled, but the smile did not make him happy inside. Many animals invited him to do cheerful things with them, including singing, swinging, rolling, strolling, resting, stomping, hugging, laughing, eating, jumping, and dancing. Jim did not want to join. He shouted and walked away. Later, he met Norman, who was also having a difficult time after getting hurt. Norman did not tell Jim to stop being grumpy. Instead, he said he would probably feel better soon. Jim said he was still grumpy and would probably feel better soon too. Accepting that feeling helped Jim feel a little better.

video_title: Too Many Pumpkins. Read Aloud Kids Books 🎃🎃🎃

summaries.summary: Rebecca Estelle grew vegetables every spring, but she never planted pumpkins. As a little girl, she had eaten pumpkins for breakfast, lunch, and dinner when her family had little money, so she hated them. One autumn, a pumpkin fell from a truck into her yard. Rebecca buried the pieces, but pumpkin vines grew from them the next spring. She cut the vines, yet they grew back. Rebecca ignored them all summer. In autumn, she discovered that pumpkins covered her whole yard. She decided to give them away, but the pumpkins were too heavy to carry. So she made pies, muffins, cakes, bread, pudding, and cookies. Then she carved funny faces into pumpkins and lit them with candles. People came to see the glowing jack-o’-lanterns. Rebecca shared the treats, seeds, and pumpkins with everyone. She even enjoyed the party and saved a few seeds for spring.

Rebecca Estelle planted many vegetables for winter, but she refused to plant pumpkins. Long ago, pumpkins had been the only food her family could afford, and she had eaten them in many ways. When a pumpkin fell from a passing truck, she buried its pieces and tried to forget them. Soon, green vines appeared. She would not water them, and she tried cutting them down, but they kept growing. By autumn, the vines had spread everywhere, and the yard was filled with pumpkins. Rebecca first planned to give the pumpkins away, but they were too heavy to deliver. She turned them into many delicious pumpkin foods. Then she carved faces in several pumpkins and placed candles inside. People from town saw the lights and came to visit. Rebecca welcomed them, shared her food, and gave each person a jack-o’-lantern, seeds, and a treat. She kept only a few seeds for planting.

video_title: Wonders Grade 5- The Case of The Missing Bees

summaries.summary: Billions of honeybees have disappeared from their colonies and never returned. This problem is called colony collapse disorder, or CCD. Because many crops need honeybees for pollination, the decline could seriously affect food production. Scientists first considered several possible causes, including crowded hives, not enough pollen, parasites, and pesticides. Researchers in Montana found both a fungus and a virus in every empty hive they tested. They concluded that either infection alone might not kill a bee, but the two together could be deadly. Other scientists think CCD may result from several factors weakening bees at the same time. Pesticides are another possible cause. Bees may consume chemicals in pollen, become confused while searching for nectar, get lost, and fail to return. Studies have found many human-made chemicals in affected hives, but scientists have not proved that pesticides directly cause CCD. More research is needed to identify the cause and protect the bees.

Honeybee colonies in many countries have suddenly disappeared, creating concern about fruits and vegetables that depend on pollination. The condition is known as colony collapse disorder. Scientists have investigated fungi, viruses, parasites, poor nutrition, crowded hives, and pesticides. A Montana study found a fungus and a virus in all the empty hives examined. The researchers believed that the combination could kill bees, even if each infection alone might not. Some scientists believe several problems could work together by weakening a bee’s immune system. Other experts focus on pesticides, which farmers spray to protect crops from harmful insects. Bees can take in these chemicals through pollen. Some pesticides may change bee behavior, causing sick bees to lose their way and never return to the hive. A study in Florida and California found fifty human-made chemicals in hives affected by CCD, but it did not prove that pesticides caused the disorder. Scientists continue investigating and may reduce harsh chemicals while searching for the answer.

The disappearance of honeybees is a serious environmental and farming problem. Billions of bees have flown away from their colonies, and the number of honeybees in the United States has fallen greatly. Since honeybees pollinate many crops, their loss could threaten food production. One possible explanation is a deadly partnership between a fungus and a virus. Infected bees might survive one illness, but bees carrying both may die. Researchers found both organisms in every empty hive in one Montana investigation. However, scientists are also studying whether pesticides, parasites, lack of pollen, and overcrowded hives contribute to CCD. Pesticides are especially suspicious because bees can consume them in pollen. Small amounts may affect how bees search for nectar, so they can become confused, get lost, and fail to return. Chemicals were found in hives in Florida and California, but a direct connection was not confirmed. Until the exact cause is known, scientists and beekeepers must continue examining the problem.

video_title: Mr Ferris and His Wheel

summaries.summary: Before the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair, people wondered how America could create something more exciting than Paris’s Eiffel Tower. Engineer George Ferris designed a giant moving wheel made of strong steel. The fair’s construction chief doubted him, and banks refused to lend him money, so Ferris used his savings and found investors. Building the wheel was difficult. Workers dug through frozen ground and dangerous quicksand before reaching solid earth. They built strong towers, added a huge axle, and connected more than 100,000 parts. On opening day, Ferris blew a golden whistle, and the enormous wheel began to turn. Passengers climbed high above the fairgrounds and saw Chicago, Lake Michigan, and distant states. Millions of people rode during the fair. The wheel survived storms, needed no repairs, and glowed at night with electric lights. After the fair, copies appeared around the world. Today, Ferris wheels remain beloved rides that make people feel as if they are flying.

George Ferris wanted to give the Chicago World’s Fair a remarkable attraction. He imagined a huge steel wheel that could move, unlike the Eiffel Tower, which stood still. Many people thought his design was too weak and complicated. Ferris struggled to find money, but he continued and ordered parts from many steel mills. His workers faced frozen ground, deep quicksand, and freezing weather. They dug down to solid ground, placed two steel towers there, and attached a giant axle. Freight trains brought over 100,000 pieces, and workers raced to assemble them. At last, the enormous circle was finished. On June 21, 1893, Ferris and his guests climbed into the first car. Two steam engines turned the wheel, lifting passengers above the fair. They saw the city, the lake, and faraway states. Visitors loved riding it, and 1.5 million passengers enjoyed it during the fair. The invention became known as the Ferris wheel and inspired wheels everywhere.

The Chicago World’s Fair needed a star attraction, so engineer George Ferris proposed a giant passenger wheel. He believed steel could make the wheel both light-looking and strong. Although the fair’s chief rejected his drawings and lenders laughed at his idea, Ferris gathered investors and began construction. Workers dug through ice and water, using pumps and steam to fight the quicksand. They built deep foundations and placed a massive axle between steel towers. Many trains delivered parts, and the crew worked day and night. The completed wheel was 265 feet high and had large passenger cars with windows and velvet seats. When Ferris blew his whistle, steam engines started the wheel. Riders climbed high over the fairgrounds and enjoyed beautiful views. The wheel carried 1.5 million people, survived strong winds, and shone with thousands of electric bulbs. After the fair ended, it was renamed the Ferris wheel. New wheels soon appeared around the world, and Ferris wheels became favorite rides at fairs and amusement parks.

They unroll a hose, and a strong spray of water sizzles against the flames. If the water tank gets empty, the pump brings water from pipes below the ground. The fire makes smoke, so the crew wears masks. A ladder rises very high and can reach a window. Soon the fire is extinguished, and all the flames are put out. The firefighters roll up their equipment and return to the station. They take a break, but the fire engine remains ready for another call.

video_title: Henry and Mudge the First Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Henry had no brothers, sisters, friends, or pets, and he felt lonely. He asked his parents for a brother, a different street, and a dog. His parents finally agreed that he could have a dog. Henry chose Mudge, a puppy with floppy ears and straight fur. Mudge grew into a very large dog. Before Mudge came, Henry worried about tornadoes, ghosts, biting dogs, and bullies on his walk to school. With Mudge beside him, Henry felt safe and happy. Mudge loved Henry’s room, his bed, and Henry himself. One day, Mudge wandered away and became lost. Henry cried, but then he knew Mudge loved him and must need help. Henry searched along roads, fields, a stream, and pine trees. When Henry called one last time, Mudge woke up and ran to him. After that, Mudge never walked away without Henry, and both friends stayed close because they never wanted to lose each other again.

Henry wanted a dog, so his parents helped him find one. The dog was named Mudge. Mudge had floppy ears and straight fur, but he was short because he was still a puppy. Soon Mudge grew very big, and he became Henry’s best friend. Henry used to hurry to school while worrying about scary things. When Mudge walked with him, Henry thought about happy things instead. Mudge loved Henry’s room and especially loved sleeping in Henry’s bed. He liked to smell Henry and then fall asleep beside him. One sunny day, Mudge went exploring without Henry. He crossed roads, a field, a stream, and pine trees, but then he could not find his way home. Henry missed him and cried. He searched everywhere, calling for Mudge. At last, Mudge heard Henry’s final call and came running. From then on, Mudge stayed close, and Henry knew he would not lose his loving dog again.

Henry felt alone because he had no brothers, sisters, friends, or pets. His parents listened when he asked for a dog, and Henry found a puppy named Mudge. Mudge had floppy ears and straight fur. Although he was small at first, he grew into a huge dog who weighed 180 pounds. Mudge made Henry feel safe. Henry began walking to school slowly and happily instead of worrying about frightening things. At home, Mudge loved Henry’s bed and slept beside him. One day, Mudge took a walk alone and became lost among roads, a field, a stream, and pine trees. Henry was very sad, but he believed Mudge loved him and must be lost. He followed the same kinds of places, calling and looking for his dog. Mudge finally woke from his lonely sleep and ran to Henry. After this, Mudge never went walking alone. Both Henry and Mudge stayed closer because they remembered how scary it was to be apart.

video_title: Read Aloud Animated Kids Books! | Vooks Narrated Storybooks

video_title: 🎅 Santa Bruce by Ryan T Higgins 📚 Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Bruce was a bear who did not like winter holidays. He liked staying in bed, but his family wanted a cozy Christmas with snow, mice, and geese. The sled carried him through the forest, where he delivered gifts to many families. By morning, every animal had a present. video_title: Give Thanks to the Lord by Karma Wilson - Children's Book Read Aloud

video_title: The Pain and the Great One - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

video_title: The Dinosaur that Pooped a Planet. Tom Fletcher & Dougie Poynter. Hilarious audiobook, read-aloud.

summaries.summary: Danny and his dinosaur are bored, so they decide to visit the science museum and fly a rocket into space. Their mummy reminds them to eat lunch, and they pack a lunchbox. The poop trail carries them back toward Earth. They land safely, and the things from space form a poop planet beside the moon. Danny promises to listen to his mummy because fun is not fun without food for your tummy. Then a Mars cat pops out of the dinosaur’s bottom.

Danny and Dinosaur are left alone in space with no way home. Danny cries until the dinosaur thinks of a plan. Dinosaur turns its poop into rocket power and sends out all the things it swallowed. The poop trail takes them back to Earth. They land safely, and the expelled space things make a poop planet near the moon. Danny says he will listen to his mummy about lunch. Then a Mars cat plops out of Dinosaur’s bottom.

Danny and Dinosaur want an exciting day, so they choose to go to space instead of doing chores. Their mummy tells them not to forget lunch. At the museum, they enter a rocket and press buttons, sending themselves high above Earth. In space, Dinosaur’s tummy rumbles. There is no lunch because Danny and Dinosaur left their packed food at home. Dinosaur eats the rocket’s gadgets and controls, then breaks outside and eats many things in space. It eats the moon, Martians, cats, satellites, stars, fuel, and finally the rocket. Danny is sad because they cannot return home. Dinosaur feels guilty and decides it must make a rocket from its bottom. It poops out the eaten things and flies toward Earth with Danny on its back. They land safely. A poop planet forms beside the moon, and Danny promises to listen to Mummy. A Mars cat appears at the very end.

video_title: ☀️🐬💨 Kids Book Read Aloud: Barbie : Little Lost Dolphin

The family thanks Barbie, and Barbie happily waves goodbye to her new friend.

Barbie enjoys the ocean, swimming, and riding her jet ski. At a lagoon, she hears a squeak and sees a baby dolphin. He is lost and cannot find his family, so Barbie decides to help him. Barbie asks a dolphin expert how to care for him. She gives him a bottle, sets up a tent, and watches him while he sleeps. The next day, Barbie’s friends visit, and the dolphin has fun jumping and playing. The dolphin still misses his family, so Barbie and her friends search again. They look near the lagoon and a cove. Then the baby hears his family squeak. The dolphins reunite, splash, and play. Barbie says goodbye happily.

Barbie rides her jet ski to a lagoon because she likes to go fast. There, she meets a baby dolphin who is swimming alone. He is lost and cannot find his family. Barbie comforts him and searches with him around the lagoon. They see fish, birds, and seaweed, but no dolphin family. When night comes, Barbie must go home, and the baby dolphin follows her. video_title: 🚶‍♀️ Kids Books Read Aloud 🚶‍♀️ The Listening Walk by Paul Showers [ READ ALONG VIDEO ]

summaries.summary: A child takes a quiet walk with Father and their old dog, Major. The child does not talk and listens carefully. First, the child hears Major’s toenails and Father’s shoes on the sidewalk. Then the child hears lawn mowers, sprinklers, cars, a bicycle bell, a crying baby, a jet, a basketball, high heels, a bus, and a loud jackhammer. The jackhammer hurts the child’s ears, so the child covers them. Sometimes Father, Major, and the child walk in the park. The park is quieter. The child hears soft footsteps, birds, pigeons, ducks, a woodpecker, crickets, wind, and bees. The child learns that listening walks can happen anywhere. You can walk around a block or a yard, or simply keep still. Sounds are everywhere all the time. At the end, the child invites listeners to close the book and count how many sounds they can hear.

The child likes taking walks with Father and an old dog named Major. During a listening walk, nobody talks. They stay still and listen to sounds around them. Major’s toenails scratch the sidewalk, and Father’s shoes make a soft, slow sound. The child hears noisy lawn mowers and quiet sprinklers. Cars make different sounds too. New cars are quiet, while old cars are noisy. The child also hears a bicycle bell, a baby, a jet, a basketball, a lady’s high heels, a bus, and a jackhammer. Later, the family walks through a quiet park. Pigeons come close, and small ducks swim near them, but big ducks stay back. The child hears a woodpecker, crickets, wind, and bees. The listening walk shows that many sounds are all around us. The child says we can listen anywhere and asks us to count sounds after closing the book.

On a walk with Father and Major, the child practices listening instead of talking. Major walks ahead and sniffs while Father keeps his hands in his pockets. The child hears toenails and shoes on the sidewalk. Along the street, many sounds appear: lawn mowers zoom, sprinklers whisper, cars make different noises, and tires and brakes make sounds. A bicycle bell rings, a baby cries, a jet flies overhead, a boy dribbles a basketball, and a lady runs to catch a bus. Men digging in the street use a jackhammer, and its banging hurts the child’s ears. In the park, everything is quieter. Pigeons and ducks come near, while the big ducks stay away. A woodpecker taps, crickets make sounds in the grass, wind whispers in leaves, and bees are in flowers. The child explains that listening does not require a long walk. We can keep still and listen to sounds everywhere.

video_title: 📚 MADDI’S FRIDGE - Kids Read Aloud Books

summaries.summary: Sophia and Maddie love playing together at the park. One day, Sophia becomes hungry and visits Maddie’s apartment for a snack. Sophia tries bringing fish and eggs in her backpack, but they make a mess. She also brings burritos, and Maddie likes them because they are good for kids and backpacks. At the climbing wall, Sophia finally reaches the top when Maddie helps her. Sophia then realizes that Maddie needs more help than she can give alone. She tells her mother, who gathers groceries for Maddie’s family. Louis even gives away his cheesy pizza bombs. Maddie is upset that Sophia broke her promise, but Sophia explains that Maddie is more important. Maddie forgives her, and they remain friends.

Maddie and Sophia are best friends who play at the park. Sophia is a fast runner, while Maddie is the best climber. Maddie says Sophia broke her promise, but Sophia says Maddie is more important. Maddie forgives her, showing that true friends help each other.

Sophia notices that her own refrigerator is full while Maddie’s refrigerator has only a few tortillas, beans, cheese, and some milk. Before this, she had tried to help by taking fish and eggs to school, but those foods were not good for backpacks. Burritos work much better, and Maddie happily eats them. Maddie also helps Sophia climb to the top of the climbing wall, proving that the girls help each other. Finally, Sophia tells her mother about Maddie’s empty refrigerator. Her mother says they will work together and fills grocery bags with food. Louis gives Maddie and Ryan his cheesy pizza bombs as a special treat. Maddie is hurt that Sophia told, but Sophia says Maddie matters more than the promise. Maddie forgives her, and the friends run upstairs together.

video_title: 🐶Arthur’s New Puppy, by Marc Brown, children’s story read aloud

summaries.summary: Arthur loved his new puppy, Pal, but Pal was very active and naughty. Pal did not like sleeping in the garage, so Arthur’s mother let him stay in the house for a few days. Pal made a cozy kitchen bed, ate quickly, ran away from his leash, and woke everyone during the night. The next morning, he made a mess in the kitchen and living room, so Mother decided that Pal should move to the garage. Arthur tried to find the garage key, but Pal had hidden it. Arthur worried that Pal might be sent away. He began training Pal with love and practiced sitting, lying down, staying, and doing tricks. At the puppy show, Pal behaved well, so the family decided he could stay. Pal then found the garage key and gave it to Arthur’s father. Arthur wanted to take Pal for another walk, but his leash had disappeared. Pal had probably hidden that, too.

Arthur was excited about his new puppy, Pal. He made Pal a home in the garage, but Pal felt lonely and ran away. Mother allowed Pal to stay in the kitchen for a short time. When the garage key disappeared, Pal could stay one more night, but Arthur heard that his parents might send him away unless he learned good behavior. Arthur trained Pal every day in the backyard. video_title: How To Catch A Star by Oliver Jeffers | Read Aloud Books for Kids

summaries.summary: A boy loved looking at the stars every night. He wished for a star of his own so it could be his friend. He imagined playing hide-and-go-seek and taking long walks with it. One morning, he tried to catch a star. He waited all day, but he could not see one until the sun was about to go away. He jumped, climbed the tallest tree, and thought about using a life preserver, a paper spaceship, or a seagull. None of these plans worked. The boy felt worried that he would never catch a star. Then he saw something floating in the water. It was a tiny star. He tried to touch it, but it rippled through his fingers. The boy felt sad, but he kept walking home. On the golden sand, he found a star that had washed ashore. At last, the boy had caught a star of his very own.

Every night, a boy watched the stars from his window. He loved them and wished that one could be his friend. He wanted to play with a star and take walks together. The boy decided to catch one. He thought morning would be a good time because a star would be tired after staying in the sky all night. At sunrise, he waited and waited. He ate lunch, waited after dinner, and finally saw a star before the sun went away. He jumped, climbed a tall tree, and tried to think of other ways to reach it. A life preserver was too heavy. His paper spaceship did not fly well. A seagull would not help him. The boy became worried and sad. Then he saw a little star in the water. It slipped through his fingers when he touched it. While walking home, he found a star on the bright golden sand. The boy had caught his own star.

A boy wanted a star very much. He watched the stars from his window each night and dreamed that one would be his friend. He thought they could play hide-and-go-seek and walk together. One day, he went outside to catch a star. He waited from sunrise until the evening. When he saw a star, he jumped for it, but he could not reach high enough. He climbed the tallest tree, but the star was still too far away. He thought about a life preserver, a paper spaceship, and a seagull. The life preserver was too heavy, the paper spaceship did not fly well, and the seagull would not help. The boy worried that he would never catch a star. Then he saw a beautiful little star floating in the water. It went through his fingers when he tried to touch it. He walked home sadly and found a star lying on the bright golden sand. video_title: FIRST DAY JITTERS Read Aloud ~ First Day of School ~ Read Along Books

video_title: The Cool Bean | Classroom Read Aloud Story Time Book for Kids | The Food Group Series

summaries.summary: The beans used to be one big, happy group, but then they stopped spending as much time together. After that, he started joining the Cool Beans at lunch, after school, and on weekends. He discovered that a smile, nod, wink, or helping hand can be truly cool.

A bean watched his old friends become the Cool Beans at school. They were admired for their talents and confident style, while he felt like a plain bean with no special skills. Soon, he began spending time with the Cool Beans again. He realized that being cool is not about appearance or popularity. It is about helping someone, lifting them up, and pointing them in the right direction.

video_title: THE LONELY PENNY by Rebecca McClantoc read aloud | kindergarten Bedtime Story | Classroom Read-Aloud

Penny travels through many hands during one unusual day. At first, she feels like a stray and wonders whether anyone wants her. A child finds her, and she goes to a wishing fountain. video_title: Pig The Tourist by Aaron Blabey, a read aloud read along story for kids by Tippy Toes Nook

Sam and Sam-I-Am talk about green eggs and ham. Sam-I-Am offers the food in many places and with many friends and animals. He says he does not like green eggs and ham and will not eat them anywhere. Sam-I-Am tells him to try them, saying that he may like them. Sam finally agrees to taste them. After trying the food, Sam says that he does like green eggs and ham. Now he would eat them in a boat, with a goat, in the rain, in the dark, on a train, in a car, in a tree, in a box, with a fox, in a house, with a mouse, here, there, and anywhere.

At the beginning, Sam says, “I am Sam,” and Sam-I-Am asks whether he likes green eggs and ham. Sam answers that he does not like them. Sam-I-Am keeps offering the meal in different places and with different companions. Sam refuses to eat it in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, in a car, in a tree, on a train, in the dark, in the rain, with a goat, or on a boat. He says he will not eat it anywhere. Then Sam-I-Am asks Sam to try the food. Sam agrees if he can be left alone, but he tastes the green eggs and ham. The taste changes his mind. Sam says the food is good and that he likes it. He will eat it in all the places and with all the companions Sam-I-Am named, and he will eat it anywhere.

video_title: Market Day | Usborne Farmyard Tales | Learn English 📚 | Learn Phonics 🔤

summaries.summary: It is Market Day, so Mrs. Boot, Poppy, and Sam put a wire crate in the trailer and drive to the market. They walk past cows, sheep, and pigs to a shed filled with birds. Mrs. Boot chooses four nice white geese and pays for them. Poppy sees a little duck that looks lonely. She asks to buy it with her own money, and Mrs. Boot says yes. When they return with the crate, the geese are placed inside. Then one goose jumps out before Sam can shut the door. The goose runs through the shed and jumps into an open car. It escapes when another door opens. Mrs. Boot tells them to run after it. The goose runs into a plant tent, where Sam catches it. Mrs. Boot takes the geese home, and Poppy takes her duck. Sam says that markets are fun.

Mrs. Boot goes to the market with Poppy and Sam to buy birds. They bring a trailer and a wire crate. At the market, they see many animals and visit a shed with cages. Mrs. Boot buys four young white geese because they look nice and friendly. Poppy notices a small duck by itself. She wants to help it and asks if she may buy it with her own money. Mrs. Boot agrees, and Poppy pays for the duck. The family brings the crate back for the geese. While Mrs. Boot puts the geese inside, one goose gets away. It jumps out, runs through the shed, and leaps into a car. When a woman opens the other car door, the goose escapes again. It runs into a plant tent. Sam catches the goose, and everyone goes home with the geese and the duck.

On Market Day, Mrs. Boot, Poppy, and Sam visit a bird market. Mrs. Boot needs four young geese, so she chooses four white ones and pays the woman selling them. Poppy looks at the other cages and sees hens, chicks, ducks, and pigeons. She feels sorry for a lonely little duck and asks to buy it with her own money. Mrs. Boot lets her do this, and Poppy pays the man. Then they return with a crate for the geese. One goose runs away before the crate door is closed. Mrs. Boot, Poppy, and Sam chase it. The goose jumps through one side of an open car and escapes through the other side when a woman opens a door. It runs into a plant tent. Sam finds it and picks it up. At last, Mrs. Boot has her geese, Poppy has her duck, and they go home.

video_title: 🏎️💨 Kids Book Read Aloud: Disney Pixar Cars : Roadwork!

Doc is ready to help cars with tune-ups. Lizzy prepares bumper stickers for her shop. Corey watches from the Lightyear blimp and reports when visitors are near. Everyone finishes the work, and the cars go out to have fun.

The cars in Radiator Springs have many jobs to do before new cars arrive. McQueen makes the road smooth. Ramone gets fresh paint. Sarge trains the four-wheel-drive visitors. Fillmore prepares his fuel, and Luigi and Guido get tires ready. Flo opens the diner, where friends can sip oil. Red cares for the flowers. Sally makes the motel ready for guests. video_title: Snow Rabbit, Spring Rabbit - Read Aloud Flip-Along Picture Book | Brightly Storytime

summaries.summary: When snow falls and the trees are bare, winter arrives. The rabbit sees that winter is here. Some gather extra food, while others travel far to find food. Some animals stay very still, and others keep moving quickly to stay warm. Then the snow melts and the trees bloom. Everyone knows that spring has come, including the rabbit. The seasons change from snowy winter to blooming spring, and animals respond to the cold in different ways.

The story begins when snow covers the ground and the trees stand bare. This tells everyone, including the rabbit, that it is winter. Animals handle winter in many ways. Some fly away from the cold. Some sleep cozily where they live. Some swim toward warmer waters. Animals with thick, woolly coats can remain in the snow. Some collect extra food, while others travel a long way to find something to eat. Some stay still, and some move fast to keep warm. At last, the snow melts and the trees are in bloom. Everyone, including the rabbit, knows that spring is here.

Winter comes when snow falls and the trees lose their leaves. The rabbit knows that the cold season has arrived. During winter, animals choose different ways to live. Some leave by flying away from the cold. Some sleep for a long, cozy time. Some swim to warmer waters. Some remain outside because their thick, woolly coats keep them warm. Some animals save extra food, and some travel far to find food. Others stay very still, while some keep busy by moving fast and staying warm. Later, the snow melts and flowers and trees bloom. This change tells everyone, including the rabbit, that winter is over and spring has begun.

video_title: The Night Before Valentine's Day Read Aloud

summaries.summary: On the night before Valentine’s Day, children in town quietly made cards. They used scissors, glittering glue, pink and red paper, paint, stickers, lace, and arrows. They wrote kind messages and put their friends’ names on the envelopes. Then they went to bed and dreamed about candy hearts. In the morning, the children carried their cards to a classroom decorated with red, pink, and white balloons and streamers. They saw a giant bouquet for their teacher and played games, including pin the heart. The art teacher painted hearts on their faces. Later, the children gave cards to Lisa, Jim, Bernard, and their other friends. Everyone read, smiled, and laughed. They ate cherries and grapes and drank fruit punch with heart-shaped ice cubes. Then the principal came dressed like Cupid. He left quickly and left a present behind. The children read his note, which wished everyone a happy Valentine’s Day.

The children were busy getting ready for Valentine’s Day. They made cards with hearts, stickers, lace, glittering glue, and bright paper. Some cards said, “You’ll be mine,” and others said, “My true valentine.” The children wrote their friends’ names on the envelopes and hoped their friends were making cards too. The next morning, the classroom looked festive with red, pink, and white decorations. A secret admirer sent the teacher a giant bouquet, and everyone knew it was from Mr. O’Meyer. The children played a heart game, laughed at silly toys, and had their faces painted with hearts. They shared their cards and enjoyed fruit, cherries, grapes, and fruit punch. Just when the party seemed finished, the principal appeared in a Cupid costume. He left a present and a note. The note said, “Happy Valentine’s Day to one and to all.”

Before Valentine’s Day, children made special cards for their friends. They cut paper, used glue and paint, added stickers and lace to giant hearts, and wrote Valentine messages. After putting names on the envelopes, they went to sleep with candy hearts in their dreams. On Valentine’s morning, they took their cards to a classroom filled with balloons and streamers. The teacher received a large bouquet from a secret admirer. The children played pin the heart, enjoyed goofy toys, and watched the art teacher paint hearts on their cheeks and other places. Then they delivered their cards. Lisa, Jim, Bernard, and the other children opened the cards, smiled, and laughed. They ate sweet cherries and grapes and drank fruit punch with heart-shaped ice cubes. At the end of the party, the principal arrived wearing Cupid’s costume. He left a present and a happy Valentine’s note for everyone.

video_title: Edwina the Dinosaur who didn't Know She was Extinct 🦕 by Mo Willems 📖 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Everyone in town knew Edua, a friendly dinosaur who played with children, helped little old ladies cross the street, and baked chocolate chip cookies. Everyone loved her except Reginald, who thought he knew everything. One day, Reginald gave a school report about extinct dinosaurs. The children said Edua could not be extinct because she was right there helping people and baking cookies. Reginald wanted to prove that dinosaurs were extinct, so he handed out flyers and protested, but nobody listened. At last, he cried. Edua told him she would listen. He took her to his classroom and explained that dinosaurs were extinct. Edua was surprised, but she understood that Reginald was right. She knew she was extinct, but she did not care. Reginald felt happy because someone had listened to him. Soon, he did not care either, and Edua continued being the friendly dinosaur everyone loved.

Edua was a dinosaur who lived in town and did kind things for everyone. She played with neighborhood children, helped little old ladies cross the street, and baked chocolate chip cookies. The townspeople loved her. Reginald did not like Edua because he wanted people to listen to what he knew. During his class report, he said that dinosaurs were extinct. The other children disagreed because Edua was alive and making cookies. Reginald decided to show the whole town that dinosaurs were extinct. He gave out flyers and tried protesting, but his plans did not work. Nobody listened, so Reginald began to cry. Edua listened when he asked. Reginald explained that all dinosaurs were extinct, and Edua realized that he was right. She knew she was extinct, but she did not mind. Reginald was pleased that Edua had listened to him, and then he stopped caring about proving his point.

Edua was a helpful dinosaur. She spent time with the neighborhood children, helped old ladies cross the street, and baked cookies for the town. Reginald believed he knew everything, so he prepared a report called “Dinosaurs Totally Extinct.” When he began speaking, the children asked about Edua. They said she could not be extinct because she was playing with them and baking cookies. Reginald became determined to prove his report was true. The next morning, he handed out flyers about extinct dinosaurs. When that failed, he protested and tried everything he could think of, but the town ignored him. Reginald cried until Edua said she would listen. In the classroom, he told her the truth about dinosaurs. His explanation was loud, expressive, and convincing. Edua was shocked, but she understood that she was extinct. She simply did not care. Reginald felt wonderful because Edua had listened to him, and soon he did not care either.

video_title: The Bruce Swap Read Along Storybook

summaries.summary: A letter arrived for Bruce the bear, inviting him to a very fun visit. Bruce did not like fun, so he said no to every exciting idea his family suggested. That night, his family secretly wished he would be more cheerful, adventurous, and full of pizzazz. The next morning, Bruce went fishing alone, while his family stayed home. Then Kevin arrived. Kevin looked like Bruce, but he was very fun. The family thought their wishes had changed grumpy Bruce into fun Bruce. Kevin and everyone else had a wonderful time at first. They ate candy, ordered too much pizza, shouted, and made a big mess. Soon the fun was not fun anymore. The family wished for regular Bruce to return, and Kevin left. When the real Bruce came home, he saw the mess and became grumpy again. Everything returned to normal, except the family got twenty-six pizzas instead of sandwiches.

Bruce was a bear who struggled with fun. He did not enjoy fun letters, silly games, unusual food, or flying in a homemade hang glider. His family became disappointed and each member made a secret wish. Thistle wished Bruce were cheerful, Rupert wished he were adventurous, Nibs wished he had pizzazz, and the geese wished for sandwiches. While Bruce went fishing, Kevin came to the house. Kevin looked just like Bruce, but he was cheerful, adventurous, and extremely fun. The family believed their wishes had swapped grumpy Bruce for Kevin. They played, ate candy, shouted, and ordered a pizza covered with more pizzas. At first, everyone loved the fun. Later, the noise and wild activities became too much, and the family wished for the real Bruce. Kevin drove away on a fun bus. Bruce returned, saw the ruined house, and decided to stop trying to have fun. The house became normal again, with one surprising delivery: twenty-six pizzas.

Bruce received an invitation from his cousin Kevin, but Bruce did not want a fun visit. He repeatedly said no when his family suggested eating sweet soup, making a yogurt sculpture, or flying a sheet hang glider. His family wished he could be more cheerful and exciting. The next day, Bruce went fishing, and Kevin arrived in his place. Because Kevin looked like Bruce, the family thought their wishes had come true. Kevin was fun, and everyone enjoyed making friends, having candy fights, shouting, and ordering enormous pizza. But the fun became noisy and dangerous. The family no longer enjoyed it and wished for ordinary Bruce to come back. Kevin left on a fun bus. When Bruce returned, he found his house in terrible condition. He briefly suggested having fun, but his family said no again and again. Bruce took them inside, saw the mess, and became grumpy. The family wanted hugs and sandwiches, while Bruce wanted bedtime. Instead, twenty-six pizzas arrived.

video_title: Pancakes, Pancakes! — 🥞 A read-aloud children's book by Eric Carle

summaries.summary: Jack wanted a big pancake for breakfast. His mother said he needed to help first. Jack cut wheat and took it to the mill. He helped separate the grain and grind it into flour. Then he fed the black hen, and she laid an egg. He milked the spotted cow and got milk. With his mother’s help, he churned the cream into butter. Jack brought firewood from the woodshed and strawberry jam from the cellar. In the kitchen, his mother mixed flour, egg, and milk in a bowl. She heated butter in a pan and poured in the batter. When the pancake was golden underneath, she flipped it high into the air and back into the pan. Soon it was crisp on both sides. His mother put it on a plate and spread jam on top. Jack knew what to do next: enjoy his big pancake.

Jack woke up hungry and asked his mother for a big pancake. She was busy, so she gave him many jobs. First, Jack cut wheat, carried it on a donkey, and helped the miller turn it into flour. Next, he fed grain to a black hen, who laid an egg. He milked a spotted cow for milk. Then Jack churned cream until it became butter. He also brought wood for the fire and found strawberry jam in the cellar. At the table, Mother showed Jack how to mix flour, egg, and milk until the batter was smooth. She cooked the batter with butter in a hot frying pan. Jack watched as she flipped the pancake into the air. It cooked until both sides were crisp. Mother placed it on a plate and added jam. Jack told her he knew what to do now.

A rooster crowed, and Jack thought about eating a large pancake. His mother said he had to help make it. Jack gathered wheat and carried it to the miller. Together they separated the grain from the straw and chaff, then ground the grain into flour. Jack got an egg from the black hen and milk from the spotted cow. He churned cream into butter, brought firewood, and picked strawberry jam from the cellar. At home, Mother put flour in a bowl, added an egg and milk, and stirred the mixture smooth. She melted butter in a frying pan and asked Jack to pour in some batter. When the bottom became golden brown, Mother flipped the pancake up and over. It landed safely in the pan. After the other side became crisp, she placed the pancake on a plate and spread strawberry jam over it. Jack said he knew what to do next.

video_title: A Picture Book of Martin Luther King, Jr  - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook - NO ADS

summaries.summary: Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta in 1929. His father was a pastor, and his mother had been a teacher. Martin loved sports, music, and reading. When he learned that white children could not play with him because he was Black, he was hurt and confused. His mother explained that Black people had once been enslaved and were still treated unfairly. Martin became a minister and later married Ketta Scott. In Montgomery, Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat, so Martin led a peaceful bus boycott. After almost a year, buses no longer had white-only sections. Martin continued peaceful protests and led the March on Washington, where he gave his “I Have a Dream” speech. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. In 1968, James Earl Ray shot and killed Martin in Memphis. Martin dreamed of a world without hate, prejudice, or violence.

Martin Luther King Jr. grew up in Atlanta with his parents, an older sister, and a younger brother. He enjoyed baseball, football, basketball, bicycling, singing, and reading about Black leaders. As a child, Martin learned that unfair rules kept Black people out of certain schools, parks, restaurants, and jobs. He worked hard in school, became a minister, and earned a doctorate. In Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks was arrested after refusing to leave her bus seat. Martin led a peaceful protest in which Black people stopped riding the buses. The protest lasted almost a year, and the buses lost their white-only sections. Martin later led marches against unfair treatment in Atlanta and organized the March on Washington in 1963. He spoke about his dream that people would be judged by their character, not skin color. He received the Nobel Peace Prize, but he was killed in 1968 while working for equal pay.

Martin Luther King Jr. saw unfair treatment of Black people when he was young, but he learned that people could work peacefully for change. He studied hard, became a pastor, and married Ketta Scott. After Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Martin helped lead a bus protest. Some followers wanted to fight after a bomb was thrown at his house, but Martin told them to go home peacefully and meet hate with love. The protest succeeded, and white-only bus sections ended. Martin moved to Atlanta and continued peaceful protests against unfair waiting rooms, lunch counters, and restrooms. In 1963, more than 200,000 people joined his March on Washington. Martin shared his dream of a nation where children would be judged by their character instead of their skin color. New laws brought greater equality, and Martin won the Nobel Peace Prize. He was killed in Memphis in 1968 while supporting equal pay for workers. His dream was a world free from hate, prejudice, and violence.

video_title: Knight Owl - Animated Read Aloud with Moving Pictures

summaries.summary: Since the day Al hatched, he wished to be a knight. He imagined being brave, clever, and having many friends. When knights began disappearing from the castle, Al went to night school and was accepted. He worked hard, even though swords and shields were difficult and he often fell asleep during the day. Al graduated with honor and became a night watchman. One very dark night, he heard a dragon. The dragon was hungry and wanted to eat him. Al was afraid, but he remembered that knights are brave and clever. He told the dragon that he was too small for a meal and suggested pizza instead. The dragon loved pizza. Al and the dragon talked about eggs, nighttime, and flying. They discovered they had much in common. After that, no more knights disappeared. Al kept patrolling the walls, and he was brave, clever, and surrounded by friends.

Al the owl wanted to become a knight from the moment he hatched. He dreamed of being brave and clever. When knights started disappearing from the castle, Al joined night school. School was not easy. He had trouble with a sword, a shield, and staying awake during the day, but he kept working. At last, he graduated with honor and received a job watching the castle walls at night. One evening, Al heard a huge whooshing sound. A hungry dragon appeared and said Al looked like a midnight snack. Al trembled, but he used bravery and clever words. He said he was too small and offered the dragon a pizza instead. The dragon liked pizza, and the two talked about the things they shared, including hatching from eggs and loving the night. Afterward, the knights stopped disappearing. Al continued his night watch and felt like a real knight with many friends.

Al had one special wish: he wanted to be a knight. He studied at night school after knights began disappearing from the castle. Although he struggled with weapons, shields, and daytime sleepiness, Al worked hard and graduated with honor. He was placed on the night watch because he could stay awake while other knights fell asleep. During one quiet night, a dragon came looking for food. The dragon said Al did not look like a knight and looked more like a snack. Al was scared, but he remembered that knights are brave. Then he remembered that knights are clever, too. He explained that he was too small to eat and suggested pizza. The dragon loved pizza. They talked together and found that they both had hatched from eggs and liked the night. From then on, no knights disappeared. Al proudly watched the castle walls because he was brave, clever, and had many friends.

video_title: Snowman Picture Story Books Collection #readaloud #kidslearning #kidsstories #picturebooks #kids

summaries.summary: Jack is building a model plane when Nancy comes to help. Jack hides because Nancy often helps, but her help sometimes changes his projects. He starts enjoying himself and understands why Nancy likes helping. Angie and Melton win the trophy, but Jack is happy to celebrate with Nancy. He tells her she is good at making snowmen, and she makes a trophy after dinner.

Jack is afraid Nancy will help with his plane, so he hides. Later, he does not let her join his snowman team. Nancy builds a snow lump by herself. When other children laugh and damage it, Jack runs to help her. Together they make a snowman. Jack’s friends leave them to work, and Jack discovers that making a snowman with Nancy is fun. The judges choose Angie and Melton as winners. Jack feels sad because he might have won with them, but Nancy takes his paw and joins the parade with him. On the way home, Jack says Nancy really is good at making snowmen. Nancy also proves that she is good at making trophies.

video_title: Snowman Picture Story Books Collection #readaloud #kidslearning #kidsstories #picturebooks #kids

summaries.summary: A snowman begins with snowflakes. Many snowflakes gather into a big ball. More snowballs make the middle and the head. One little snowflake falls from the sky. Then thousands, millions, and billions more join it. The snow is patted, packed, and rolled into a large ball. To make a snowman, first gather lots of soft snow. Roll it into a big ball, then make a middle ball and a small head. Put on a hat. Add bottle-cap eyes, a carrot nose, buttons, boots, and a scarf. Give him mittens, earmuffs, and other useful things. Then look up. Snow keeps falling everywhere, and the new snow makes a friend for the snowman.

video_title: Toy Story 🤠 Read Along Storybook 📖 Read Aloud Stories for Kids

summaries.summary: It is Easter morning, and Bonnie finds an Easter basket. The basket is full of surprises, including candy, eggs, and jelly beans. On Easter morning, Bonnie finds a basket filled with candy, eggs, and jelly beans. The toys find a bunny in the basket. They think it is a new toy, so they try many ways to play with it. Woody says hello. Mr. Potato Head makes a funny face. Mr. Prickle Pants sings and dances. Rex and Trixie play a game. Dolly has a tea party. Buzz sounds his laser. Bonnie’s Easter basket has candy, eggs, jelly beans, and a bunny. The toys see the bunny and believe it is a new toy. Woody greets it, but the bunny does not say hello. Mr. Potato Head makes a funny face, but there is no giggle. Mr. Prickle Pants sings and dances, but there is no clap or cheer. Rex and Trixie play a game, but the bunny does not play alone. Dolly offers a tea party, but the bunny does not sip tea. Buzz uses his laser sound, but the bunny does not wake up. Bonnie arrives and bites the bunny’s ear. The toys are shocked when they see the truth. The bunny is chocolate. It is not a toy. Everyone laughs together. The Easter basket has brought a surprising bunny to the toys.

video_title: Parts

The child says that each day brings something worse. At first, hair is found in the comb, and the child thinks baldness is beginning. Later, fuzz comes out, and the child believes the body may be stuffed. Skin peels from the toes, so the child imagines being reduced to bones. A gray, wet piece falls from the nose, and the child wonders whether it is brain. When a tooth starts to come loose, the child worries about eating and imagines the body coming apart. The child thinks an ear, an eyeball, an arm, or a head could fall off and pictures being left in a shapeless pile. Dad then gives important information: teeth fall out, and new teeth grow in. Hair, skin, and everything else are normal, so the child is relieved. Still, the child has one more question about yellow stuff from the ear.

video_title: Margret and H A  Reys Merry Christmas Curious George kids book read along

summaries.summary: George visits a Christmas tree farm with the Man with the Yellow Hat. He promises to stay close, but many trees make him curious. George climbs the tallest tree. Curious George wants to help choose a Christmas tree, but he keeps looking at more trees. He climbs a very tall one to see everything. summaries.summary: George’s mother wants George to bark like a dog. She asks him again and again, but George says no. She explains that cats say “Wow,” dogs say “Arf,” ducks say “Quack quack,” and pigs say “Oink oink.” George still does not bark, so his mother takes him to the vet. The vet asks George to bark and reaches deep inside him. The vet pulls out a cat, then a duck, then a pig, and keeps looking. At last, George barks. George’s mother is very happy. She kisses the vet, the cat, the duck, the pig, and the cow. On the way home, she proudly asks George to bark for everyone. This time, George says, “Hello.”

George does not bark when his mother asks him to. His mother tells him that cats go “Wow,” dogs go “Arf,” ducks go “Quack quack,” and pigs go “Oink oink.” George still says no, so she takes him to see the vet. The vet thinks he can find the problem. He asks George to bark and reaches deep inside George. First, he pulls out a cat. Then he pulls out a duck. Next, he pulls out a pig. The vet reaches farther inside George and keeps trying. Finally, George barks. George’s mother is thrilled and kisses the vet and the animals. Then she takes George home and wants everyone in the street to hear him bark. When she asks, “Bark, George?” George answers, “Hello.”

George’s mother wants her dog to make a dog sound, but George will not bark. She reminds him that cats, dogs, ducks, and pigs make different sounds. George continues to say no, so his mother brings him to the vet. The vet says he will get to the bottom of the mystery. When George is asked to bark, the vet reaches inside him and pulls out a cat. He asks George to bark again and pulls out a duck. He asks once more and pulls out a pig. The vet reaches very deep inside George and finally gets George to bark. George’s mother is delighted. She kisses the vet and the animals, including the cow. While walking home, she wants to show George to everyone. She asks him to bark one more time. Instead of barking, George says, “Hello.”

video_title: Guji Guji

summaries.summary: An egg rolled through the trees, across a meadow, and down a hill into Mother Duck’s nest. Four ducklings hatched. One had blue spots, one had brown stripes, one was yellow, and the fourth was an odd-looking duckling named GUI GUI. Mother Duck taught them to swim, dive, and waddle. GUI GUI learned quickly and grew big and strong, but Mother Duck loved all four ducklings equally. One day, three crocodiles came from the lake. They told GUI GUI that he was a crocodile and asked him to bring the ducks to the bridge. They planned to eat them. GUI GUI felt worried, but he made a plan. He brought the ducks to the bridge, but dropped three hard rocks instead. The crocodiles bit the rocks and broke their teeth. They ran away, and GUI GUI saved the ducks. Everyone celebrated, and GUI GUI lived happily with his duck family.

A rolling egg found its way into a duck’s nest. Soon, four ducklings came out. Mother Duck named them Crayon, Zebra, Moonlight, and GUI GUI. She taught them to swim, dive, and waddle. GUI GUI was bigger, stronger, and quicker than the others, but Mother Duck loved every duckling the same. Then three crocodiles saw GUI GUI. They said he looked like them because he had blue-gray skin, claws, and pointed teeth. The crocodiles wanted him to take the ducks to a bridge so they could eat them. GUI GUI wondered if he was a bad crocodile, but he knew the crocodiles were nasty and wanted to harm his family. He thought of a clever idea. At the bridge, GUI GUI dropped three big rocks instead of ducks. The crocodiles bit the rocks and broke their teeth. They ran away, and the ducks celebrated GUI GUI as their hero.

Mother Duck did not notice an egg rolling into her nest. Four ducklings hatched from the eggs. Crayon had blue spots, Zebra had brown stripes, Moonlight was yellow, and GUI GUI looked different. Mother Duck taught all of them how to swim, dive, and waddle. GUI GUI learned fast and became strong, while Mother Duck loved all the ducklings equally. One day, three crocodiles tried to trick GUI GUI. They said he was a crocodile too and asked him to bring the ducks to the bridge. They waited underneath so they could eat the ducks. GUI GUI felt terrible and looked at his face in the lake. He knew he was not a bad crocodile, and he wanted to protect his family. The next day, he brought the ducks to the bridge, but three hard rocks fell down instead. The crocodiles broke their teeth on the rocks and ran away. GUI GUI saved the ducks and became their hero.

video_title: The Jungle Book Read Along Storybook, Read Aloud Story Books, Books Stories, Bedtime Stories

summaries.summary: Mowgli is a little boy who lives with wolves in the jungle. Bagheera the panther finds him and takes him to the wolf family. Mowgli loves the wolves and thinks they are his brothers. One day, the tiger Shere Khan comes back. The wolves say Mowgli must go to the man village to be safe. Mowgli does not want to leave. He runs away and meets a baby elephant, then plays with Baloo the bear. Monkeys capture Mowgli and take him to King Louie. Bagheera and Baloo rescue him. Mowgli runs away again and meets Shere Khan. When lightning starts a fire, Mowgli uses a burning branch to scare the tiger away. Then Mowgli understands that the jungle is dangerous. He goes with Bagheera and Baloo toward the man village. A village girl sings by the river, and Mowgli follows her into the village. His friends watch him go, then return to the jungle.

A baby named Mowgli grows up with a wolf family in the jungle. He loves his wolf brothers. When Shere Khan, the tiger, returns, the wolf leader says Mowgli must leave so he will be safe. Bagheera takes Mowgli toward the man village, but Mowgli runs away. He marches with elephants and later plays with Baloo the bear. The jungle has danger everywhere. Monkeys grab Mowgli and carry him to their ruined city. King Louie wants Mowgli to tell him about man's red fire. Bagheera and Baloo rescue Mowgli. Mowgli runs away again and finds Shere Khan. The tiger tries to attack, but lightning sets a tree on fire. Mowgli ties a burning branch to the tiger's tail, and Shere Khan runs away. Mowgli learns that the jungle is not safe for him. He follows a village girl into the man village. Baloo and Bagheera say goodbye and walk back into the jungle.

Mowgli lives happily with wolves after Bagheera brings him to their den. He calls the wolves his family. Then Shere Khan comes to the jungle, and the wolves decide Mowgli should go to the man village. Mowgli wants to stay, so he leaves Bagheera and meets elephants. He also meets Baloo, who shares jungle food and fun with him. Soon, monkeys carry Mowgli away. Bagheera and Baloo hurry to the monkeys' ruined city and save him from King Louie. Mowgli becomes upset and runs off alone. Shere Khan finds him and prepares to pounce. A nearby tree catches fire during lightning. Mowgli takes a burning branch and scares the tiger away. Now Mowgli knows he needs a safer home. The next morning, he travels with Bagheera and Baloo. A girl sings as she carries water from the river. Mowgli follows her through the village gates, while his two friends watch and then return to the jungle.

video_title: Snow White And The Seven Dwarfs@Readingtimewithnana

summaries.summary: A kind girl named Snow White is born after a queen wishes for a daughter with snowy skin, red lips, and black hair. Snow White’s mother dies, and her father marries a beautiful but cruel queen. The new queen loves her magic mirror and wants to be the fairest woman in the kingdom. When the mirror says Snow White is fairest, the queen becomes angry and sends a huntsman to kill her. The huntsman feels sorry for Snow White and lets her run into the forest. There, woodland animals lead her to a little house belonging to seven dwarfs. Snow White cleans the house and stays with them. The queen disguises herself as an old woman and gives Snow White a poisoned apple. Snow White falls asleep, but a prince kisses her and she wakes up. The dwarfs rejoice, and the prince takes Snow White to his castle.

Long ago, a baby girl called Snow White was born to a loving queen. After her mother died, Snow White lived with a new queen who was proud, jealous, and cruel. The new queen asked her magic mirror who was the fairest. One day, the mirror named Snow White instead of the queen. The queen ordered a huntsman to take Snow White into the forest, but he could not hurt her. Snow White wandered through the woods and found a small, messy house. Friendly animals helped her clean it. The house belonged to seven dwarfs named Dopey, Sneezy, Happy, Grumpy, Doc, Bashful, and Sleepy. They invited Snow White to stay. The queen later came to the house in disguise with a poisoned apple. Snow White ate it and fell lifeless. The dwarfs watched over her until a prince came. He kissed Snow White, and she woke up. Then he carried her to his castle.

Snow White was a beautiful and gentle princess, and everyone loved her except her jealous stepmother. The stepmother spent much time admiring herself in a magic mirror. She wanted to be the most beautiful woman in the kingdom. When the mirror said that Snow White was fairest, the queen became furious. She sent Snow White away with a huntsman, but he told the princess to hide in the forest. Snow White cried, and then woodland animals helped her find a tiny house. She cleaned the house and fell asleep on one of seven little beds. The seven dwarfs came home, discovered her, and welcomed her. They loved her merry ways and warned her not to speak to strangers. The queen disguised herself as an old woman and offered Snow White a magic poisoned apple. Snow White took a bite and fell down. The queen disappeared, and the dwarfs kept watch. A handsome prince found Snow White and kissed her. She woke up, and the dwarfs danced happily.

video_title: The Three Little Pigs - Read Aloud Flip-Along Picture Book | Brightly Storytime

summaries.summary: An old sao sent her three little pigs into the world. The first pig built a house from straw, and the second built a house from sticks. A hungry wolf came to each house. He huffed and puffed, blew each house down, and gobbled up each little pig. The third pig built a strong house from bricks. The wolf could not blow it down, so he tried tricks. The clever pig gathered turnips before the wolf arrived and picked apples before the wolf could catch him. At a fair, the pig hid inside a butter churn and rolled down the hill. The wolf became frightened and ran home. Later, the angry wolf climbed onto the brick house roof. The third pig made a fire under a big iron pot. When the wolf came down, the pig cooked and gobbled him up.

Three little pigs left home to seek their fortunes. The first pig used straw, and the second pig used sticks because their houses were quick to build. A hungry wolf visited them. He huffed and puffed, blew down both houses, and ate both pigs. The third pig took longer to build a sturdy brick house. The wolf tried to blow it down, but the brick house stood firm. Then the wolf made plans to meet the pig for turnips, apples, and a fair. Each time, the pig went first and escaped. He picked turnips, gathered apples, and rolled down the hill inside a butter churn. The wolf ran away in fear. Later, the wolf climbed onto the brick house roof and said he would eat the pig. The pig prepared a hot iron pot. The wolf came down, and the pig cooked and ate him.

An old sao told her three little pigs that she loved them, then sent them out into the world. Two pigs chose fast houses made from straw and sticks. The hungry wolf blew both houses down and gobbled up those pigs. The third pig worked hard and built a solid brick house. The wolf could not blow it down, so he tried to trick the pig. The pig was ready each time. He gathered turnips before the wolf arrived, escaped from the apple tree, and used a butter churn to roll safely away from the fair. The wolf was frightened by the rolling churn and ran home. That night, he climbed onto the brick house roof. The third pig quickly made a fire and put a big iron pot over it. When the wolf came down, the pig cooked the mean old wolf and gobbled him up.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: North American Indians by Marie and Douglas Gorsline

summaries.summary: Thousands of years ago, the first people came to America from Asia. By the time Columbus arrived, many Indian tribes lived across the land and spoke different languages. European settlers met these tribes, sometimes sharing knowledge and sometimes fighting over land. The story describes how different tribes lived. Algonquian people hunted and fished near the Atlantic and lived in wigwams. The Seminoles lived in Florida swamps, while the Iroquois lived in long houses. Plains tribes followed buffalo herds, using horses, hides, bones, and every part of the animals. Pueblo people built adobe homes and grew crops in dry places. Apache people hunted, and Navajo people raised sheep and made blankets. Northwest Coast tribes fished, hunted whales, carved totem poles, and held feasts. Indian languages gave names to many places. Plains tribes also used sign language and smoke signals to communicate.

The book explains the lives of many North American Indian tribes. The Algonquians lived along the Atlantic coast in bark-covered wigwams and learned to grow corn and squash. Seminoles moved into Florida swamps and built houses on stilts. Iroquois families shared large long houses and grew corn. Ojibwes traveled by canoe to hunt, fish, and gather wild rice. On the Great Plains, tribes hunted buffalo. After horses arrived, groups such as the Sioux could follow buffalo herds and carry heavy loads. Buffalo provided meat, clothing, tools, shelters, and many other useful things. Pueblo Indians built homes from adobe and stone, farmed, made pottery, and danced for rain and good crops. Apaches raided for food, while Navajos raised sheep and wove blankets. Northwest Coast Indians used fish, forests, and whales. They built plank houses, canoes, and totem poles. Tribes also communicated with sign language and smoke signals.

Long ago, many Indian tribes lived in different parts of North America. Each tribe had its own language and way of life. Coastal tribes hunted and fished, made wigwams, and used wampum beads. Tribes around the Great Lakes lived in long houses or traveled in canoes. Plains Indians depended greatly on buffalo. They hunted buffalo on foot and later used horses to follow whole herds. They ate the meat and used the hides, bones, horns, and hoofs for food, clothing, homes, tools, and other objects. Children learned by helping their families. In the Southwest, Pueblo people built strong adobe homes, grew crops, made pottery, and held dances. Apache people gathered food and took horses, while Navajos settled down, raised sheep, and made wool blankets. Northwest Coast people used wood, fish, and whales. They built boats and houses, carved totem poles, and held gift-giving feasts. Indian languages also influenced many American place names.

video_title: The Tiny Seed by Eric Carle

summaries.summary: In autumn, a strong wind carries many flower seeds across the land. The Tiny Seed is smaller and slower than the others. Some seeds are burned by the sun, frozen on a mountain, drowned in the ocean, or left in the hot desert. The Tiny Seed survives. A bird and a mouse do not see it, so it rests safely through winter. In spring, the seeds open and grow roots, stems, and leaves. A weed takes sunlight and rain from one little plant, and a child breaks another. The Tiny Seed finally grows, but flowers and plants around it are damaged or picked. The Tiny Plant keeps growing through summer. It becomes taller than people, trees, and houses. A giant flower grows, and birds, bees, and butterflies visit it. In autumn, the wind shakes the flower. Its seed pod opens, and many tiny seeds fly away.

A tiny flower seed travels with the wind in autumn. It is smaller and slower than the other seeds, but it keeps flying. Along the way, seeds are lost because the hot sun burns one, ice traps one, water drowns one, and desert heat stops another. When the seeds land, a bird eats one, but the Tiny Seed is too small to see. Snow covers it during winter, and a mouse eats another seed without finding the Tiny Seed. Spring brings sunshine, rain, and warm air. The Tiny Seed opens and sends roots down and a stem up. A big weed kills one small plant, and a child breaks another. A boy picks a flower from a faster-growing plant. The Tiny Plant grows alone all summer. It becomes a huge flower taller than houses. Birds, bees, and butterflies visit. When autumn returns, its seed pod opens, sending many new seeds into the wind.

The Tiny Seed begins a long journey with many flower seeds. It travels over land and water while other seeds disappear in the sun, on an icy mountain, in the ocean, and in the desert. The Tiny Seed lands safely and hides from a bird and a hungry mouse. It sleeps under snow until spring. Then sunshine and rain help the seeds open. They grow roots, stems, and leaves. Some young plants do not survive: a weed takes away light and rain, and a child breaks another plant. The Tiny Seed is slow to start, but it begins growing at last. A faster plant grows a flower, but a boy picks it. The Tiny Plant continues growing by itself. It becomes taller than people, trees, and houses, and makes a giant flower. Birds, bees, and butterflies visit the beautiful flower. Autumn comes again. Strong wind shakes the flower, its seed pod opens, and many tiny seeds sail away.
