The lion teacher gives a student seven lessons. The student stretches, tries to look fierce, and roars into a microphone. The lion says the roaring needs work. At lunchtime, the student wants spaghetti, but the lion explains that lions do not eat spaghetti and lists several lion foods. Next, they creep through the woods. The student hides in bushes and behind trees, yet the lion can still see the tail. The student must also run to a faraway hill, but the trip takes an hour. Then the student gets a running start and pounces on a lady. Instead of being frightened, she calls the student a cute little kitty cat. The final lesson is looking out for friends. The student knows a kitten is a friend and chases a dog with a fierce roar, claws, teeth, and a pounce. The lion says, “Bravo!” The student gets a diploma, but the neighborhood cats will not leave the student alone.

video_title: ♾️ Math Curse

summaries.summary: On Monday, Miss Fibonacci tells the class that almost everything can be a math problem. The next day, a child begins seeing math everywhere. Getting ready for school brings questions about time, shirts, milk, and measurements. The bus, birthday chart, classroom desks, lunch, and every subject at school become math problems too. Even pizza, pie, geography, words, baseball, art, and different ways of counting seem impossible. By the end of the day, the child feels like a math zombie. At home, candy, money, a whole year, dinner, and even bedtime turn into more problems. In a dream, the child is trapped in a room covered with problems. The child breaks a piece of chalk in half and uses one half plus one half to make a whole, then escapes. On Wednesday morning, the child solves the time problem easily and feels free from the math curse—until science class begins.

A child’s ordinary day changes after Miss Fibonacci says that almost everything can be thought of as a math problem. The child worries about waking up, dressing, eating, brushing teeth, catching the bus, counting shirts, and measuring milk. At school, questions appear in every class. The child counts children, fingers, ears, and tongues, thinks about fractions in pizza and pie, estimates the length of the Mississippi River with candy, solves word and baseball questions, and studies unusual number systems. Birthday cupcakes create another fraction problem, so the child says, “I’m allergic to cupcakes,” and everyone gets one cupcake. After school, money and a confusing family statement create more puzzles. During sleep, the child is locked in a room full of problems. Remembering fractions, the child breaks chalk in half, puts the halves together to make one whole, and escapes. The next morning, the child solves the schedule problem and breaks the curse, but science brings a new challenge.

Miss Fibonacci tells her students that many things can be math problems, and one child takes the idea very seriously. The child notices problems in the morning routine, clothing, breakfast, transportation, birthdays, classroom arrangements, lunch, geography, English, sports, art, and number sequences. The child becomes so overwhelmed that school feels like a math curse. When Rebecca brings 24 cupcakes for 24 children but wants one for the teacher too, the class struggles with fractions. The child avoids the problem by claiming an allergy, so each student gets one cupcake. At home, the child faces problems about a sale, bills, coins, a year of minutes, and whether the parents’ statements can both be true. Before sleeping, the child counts sheep with more arithmetic. In a dream, the child is trapped in a room with endless problems and only one piece of chalk. Breaking the chalk into two halves gives the answer: one half plus one half equals one whole. The child escapes and wakes up cured of the math curse.

video_title: 🐢👻🎃Franklin’s Halloween by Paulette Bourgeois and Brenda Clark, kids story, read aloud

summaries.summary: Franklin was excited for Halloween because his friends were having a costume party with games, prizes, a parade, and a haunted house. He made a creepy costume and called himself Frankinstein. At the party, he played apple bobbing and pumpkin toss, then won a prize for being the best green monster. Franklin entered the haunted house and became frightened when a hairy hand reached from the darkness. The hand belonged to Mr. Mole, who explained that the ghost Franklin had seen was not Bear, because Bear was sick at home. Franklin and his friends watched the ghost fly low and say, “Wo.” Franklin noticed a feather and guessed that Mr. Owl was pretending to be a ghost. At the end of the party, the friends filled a bag with treats for Bear and left it at his doorstep. Franklin went home with many treats and hoped they would last until the end of the week.

On Halloween, Franklin and his friends went to a costume party. Franklin could not decide what to wear, so he made a creepy costume and dressed as Frankinstein. At the party, he tried apple bobbing, played pumpkin toss, and joined the costume parade. He made monster sounds and shuffled like a monster, so he won a prize for being the best green monster. Then Beaver pushed him into the haunted house. Inside, chains rattled, moans sounded, and a hairy hand grabbed out of the darkness. Franklin was scared, but the light showed that Mr. Mole was holding a mop. Mr. Mole said a ghost had come before Franklin and flown away. Franklin learned that Bear was sick at home, so the ghost had to be someone else. A feather helped Franklin discover that Mr. Owl had played the trick. The friends shared their treats with Bear.

Franklin knew Halloween was October 31st, and he looked forward to the party with all his friends. He made a green monster costume because Fox told him to look for something gruesome. At the party, Franklin guessed that Bear was dressed as a ghost, but the ghost was really Mr. Owl. Franklin did not know this yet. He played games, filled his treat bag, and won a costume prize. When he entered the haunted house, he heard scary sounds and felt a hairy hand. The hand belonged to Mr. Mole and his mop. Mr. Mole said the ghost had flown away, and Franklin realized that Bear could not have been the ghost because Bear was home with a cold. Franklin saw a feather floating down and guessed the truth. His friends agreed that Mr. Owl was the ghost. They shared their candy with Bear, then Franklin went home with treats.

video_title: The Princess And The Pea@Readingtimewithnana

summaries.summary: A prince wanted to marry a real princess, so he traveled around the world looking for one. He met many princesses, but something about each one did not seem right. He went home feeling unhappy. One stormy night, a girl came to the city gate. She was wet from the rain and said she was a real princess. The old queen made a test. She put one pea on a bed, placed 20 mattresses on top, and added 20 feather beds. The princess slept on the tall bed. In the morning, she said she had hardly slept because something hard had made her black and blue. The family knew she had felt the pea through all the beds. They decided she was a real princess. The prince asked her to marry him, and the pea was placed in the royal museum.

Once, a prince searched everywhere for a real princess to marry. Many princesses came, but he could not tell if they were real, so he returned home unhappy. Then a terrible storm came. During the storm, a princess knocked at the city gate. Rain had soaked her hair, clothes, and shoes, but she still said she was a real princess. The old queen wanted to find out. She put a pea on a mattress, piled 20 more mattresses above it, and placed 20 feather beds on top. The princess slept there for the night. In the morning, she said she had slept badly and felt something so hard that she was black and blue. The king, queen, and princess saw that she had felt the pea through every mattress and feather bed. The prince knew she was real and asked her to marry him. The pea went to the royal museum.

A prince wished to find a real princess, but his journeys brought him no answer. He returned to the king and queen feeling unhappy. One night, thunder, lightning, and heavy rain came to the castle. A princess arrived at the city gate, soaked by the storm. She said she was a real princess. The old queen made a secret test for her. She placed a pea on the mattress, added 20 mattresses, and then added 20 feather beds. The princess spent the night on top. When morning came, the queen asked whether she had slept well. The princess said she had hardly slept because a hard thing had hurt her so much that she was black and blue. The family understood that she had felt the pea beneath all the beds. They decided she was a real princess. The prince asked her to marry him, and the pea was kept in the royal museum.

video_title: Mickey Mouse Clubhouse - My First Colors 📖 Read Along Story books 📚 Read Aloud Stories for Kids

summaries.summary: Minnie sees a rainbow in her book and asks about its colors. Mickey looks for red things, such as a car, berries, and a stop sign. At the end, rain comes, and the pals cheer when a beautiful rainbow appears.

Minnie points to a rainbow in her book. The friends look closely at colors all around them. Mickey finds red in a car, berries, and a stop sign. Goofy finds orange in a tiger’s fur and butterfly wings. Pluto finds yellow in the Sun and little ducklings. Minnie finds green peas and cucumbers. Donald finds blue blueberry juice and a bluebird. Daisy finds purple lilacs and violets. After finding colors, Mickey uses red, yellow, and blue paints. The friends think about which colors can be mixed to make orange, green, and purple. Minnie strings beads in rainbow colors and asks for help finding the colors. They also look at color patterns and decide what color comes next. Then the day turns to rain. The pals cheer together when a beautiful rainbow begins to appear.

A rainbow is waiting in Minnie’s book, so the friends begin a color search. They look for red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple. Mickey sees a red car, berries, and a stop sign. They learn about mixing two colors to make orange, green, and purple. Minnie strings rainbow beads, and the friends study patterns to find the next color. Rain comes at the end, and everyone cheers as a beautiful rainbow appears.

video_title: Malala's Magic Pencil by Malala Yousafzai | Read Aloud Books for Kids

summaries.summary: When Malala was young, she wished for a magic pencil like one she saw on television. She wanted to help her family, make beautiful things for her mother, build schools for her father, and make the world better. One day, she saw children working at a trash dump instead of going to school. Her father explained that some children had to work, and many girls were not allowed to attend school. Malala began to understand how lucky she was and wished for peace, food, and equal chances for girls and boys. Later, dangerous men stopped girls in her valley from going to school. Malala wrote about what was happening, gave speeches, and shared her story. The men tried to silence her, but people around the world joined her. Malala discovered that her words and work were the magic she had been seeking. She continued working for peace and said that one child, one teacher, one book, and one pen can change the world.

Malala once dreamed of having a magic pencil. She imagined using it to stop time, remove the smell of the trash dump, make dresses for her mother, help her father build schools, and give her brothers a real ball. Every morning, she looked for the pencil, but it never appeared. At a dump, Malala saw a girl and boys sorting through rubbish for useful scraps. Her father told her that some children worked because their families needed food, and many girls could not go to school. Malala decided that her magic pencil would create a peaceful world without war, poverty, or hunger, where girls and boys were equals. Then dangerous men made girls afraid to attend school. Malala began writing about the problem and speaking for girls who could not speak for themselves. Her voice reached people in many countries. She learned that words, courage, and hard work could help change the world.

Malala loved school and wanted every child to have the same chance to learn. As a child, she imagined a magic pencil that could solve problems and make people happy. After seeing children working at a dump, she learned that some families needed their children to work and that many girls were kept out of school. She thought about how girls in her country were often expected to cook and clean instead of following their dreams. Malala worked hard in school, but dangerous men later declared that girls could not attend. Many students stopped coming because they were scared. Malala chose to speak out. She wrote about the fear, her love of school, and the lives of girls in her valley. She gave speeches and talked with a reporter. Although the dangerous men tried to silence her, people joined her, and her message became louder. Malala found magic in her words and work and kept trying to make the world peaceful.

video_title: How To Catch Santa Read Aloud

summaries.summary: After waiting many days, Christmas Eve finally arrives, and a child plans to catch Santa. The child thinks of questions to ask, such as how Santa travels so quickly, how he uses chimneys, and how he finds children who are away. Glitter, carrots, riddles, cookies, arrows, bells, and Christmas lights may reveal that Santa has visited. While waiting, the child listens for sleigh bells, reindeer, elves, and Santa’s laugh. Before bed, the child leaves clues, asks a puppy to watch, and looks out the window one last time. Santa will come only after the child falls asleep. Even if Santa is not caught this year, there will always be another Christmas.

On Christmas Eve, a child decides to try to catch Santa, knowing Santa will not stay long. The child prepares questions about chimneys, reindeer, elves, letters, toys, and cookies. The child also wants to tell Santa about trying to be good and give him special gifts. The plan is to be clever, gentle, and patient rather than using nets or snow traps. The child makes clues by putting glitter in a note, leaving carrots for the reindeer, writing riddles, and guiding Santa toward the child’s room. Bells above the cookies might make a sound when Santa arrives. As night comes, the family watches and listens for Santa’s sounds. The child leaves the tree lights on, places the riddles nearby, and lets a gentle puppy stay in the bedroom. Then the child peeks outside and goes to sleep, hoping to catch Santa.

The story explains how to prepare for Santa’s visit. First, a child thinks of many questions, messages, and gifts for Santa and Mrs. Claus. Next, the child makes a careful catching plan. The child avoids dangerous or silly ideas and instead uses glitter, carrots, cookies, riddles, arrows, bells, and Christmas lights. These objects can leave clues or help the child notice Santa’s visit. While waiting, the child sings songs, reads books, and asks family members whether they ever tried to catch Santa. When it gets dark, Santa and his reindeer begin traveling. The family watches the windows and listens for sleigh bells, reindeer, elves, and Santa saying “ho ho ho.” When the child becomes sleepy, the final preparations are made. A puppy may watch gently, but Santa will not arrive until the child is asleep. The child looks outside one last time. Catching Santa may happen next year if it does not happen tonight.

video_title: Tiny One | A Classic English Fairy Tale | Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: Long ago in Japan, a man and his wife wished for a baby. The wife said she did not mind how small the baby was, and soon they found a tiny baby on their doorstep. They called him Tiny One. He grew into a man, but he stayed very small. Tiny One wanted to seek his fortune, so he traveled down the river in a rice bowl, using chopsticks as oars and a sewing needle as a sword. He reached the emperor’s palace and became the emperor’s daughter’s companion. One day, a red ogre grabbed the emperor’s daughter. Tiny One bravely attacked the ogre’s tongue with his needle. The ogre dropped him and ran away, leaving a magic stick behind. Tiny One used the stick to wish to become bigger and taller. His wish came true, and he married the emperor’s daughter. They lived happily ever after.

A man and his wife in Japan wished for a child, and a tiny baby appeared on their doorstep. The wife named him Tiny One. Although he grew up, he did not become much bigger. When he became a man, he decided to seek his fortune. He sailed down the river in a rice bowl, rowed with chopsticks, and carried a sewing needle for a sword. He arrived at the emperor’s palace and secretly entered the throne room. The emperor liked him and asked him to stay as his daughter’s companion. Later, a red ogre seized the emperor’s daughter in the garden. Tiny One shouted for the ogre to let her go. When the ogre tried to eat him, Tiny One jabbed the ogre’s tongue with his needle. The ogre ran away and left a magic stick. Tiny One wished to be tall and big, and then married the emperor’s daughter.

Tiny One was a very small child whose wishful parents found him on their doorstep. They loved him and gave him his name. As an adult, Tiny One wanted to find his fortune, so he made a boat from a rice bowl. He used chopsticks to row and took a sewing needle as a sword. After traveling for a week, he reached the emperor’s palace. He slipped under the door and climbed onto the emperor’s knee. The emperor welcomed him and made him his daughter’s companion. One day, a red ogre appeared while Tiny One and the princess walked in the garden. The ogre grabbed the princess and laughed at Tiny One because he was so small. When the ogre put Tiny One in his mouth, Tiny One used his needle to hurt the ogre’s tongue. The ogre fled, leaving a magic stick. Tiny One wished to become bigger and taller, and his wish came true. He and the emperor’s daughter married and were happy.

video_title: Grumpy Monkey 🐵 .Read Aloud Kids Book

summaries.summary: One wonderful day, Jim woke up and felt that everything was wrong. The sun was too bright, the sky was too blue, and the bananas were too sweet. Norman said Jim might be grumpy, but Jim said he was not. Other animals noticed that Jim looked grumpy because he stood hunched, bunched his eyebrows, and frowned. Jim did not want to do any of those things. He shouted and stormed away. Then Jim found Norman looking grumpy too. Norman had danced with a porcupine, and he hurt. Norman said he would feel better soon. Jim said he was grumpy too and needed time. Norman agreed, and Jim already felt a little better.

Jim woke on a beautiful day, but he did not feel happy. He thought the sun was too bright, the sky was too blue, and the bananas were too sweet. Norman guessed that Jim was grumpy. Jim kept saying he was not grumpy, even when Marabou, Lemur, Snake, and Norman saw his hunched body, bunched eyebrows, and frown. Jim made a smile, but the smile did not change how he felt inside. Many animals invited Jim to sing, swing, roll, stroll, stomp, splash, hug, laugh, nap, eat, jump, sit in the sun, and dance. Jim did not feel like doing anything. He shouted and walked away. Later, he saw Norman looking sad and grumpy. Norman explained that a dance with a porcupine hurt him, but he would feel better soon. Jim admitted that he was grumpy. Norman said it was all right to be grumpy for now, and Jim began to feel better.

Jim began his day feeling upset, although the day was wonderful. He said he was not grumpy, but his body, eyebrows, and face showed that he was. The animals tried to help by inviting him to sing, swing, roll, stroll, lie in the grass, stomp, splash, hug, laugh, nap, eat, jump, sit in the sun, and dance. Jim did not want to join them. He shouted, beat his chest, and stormed off. Jim felt a little sorry for shouting, but he mostly felt sorry for himself. Then he met Norman. Norman was slumped, had bunched eyebrows, and was frowning. Norman said he had danced with a porcupine, so he was hurting. He believed he would feel better soon. Jim said he was still grumpy and would probably feel better soon too. Norman told Jim that it was a wonderful day to be grumpy. Jim agreed, and he felt a little better.

video_title: GOD GAVE US EASTER Read Aloud ~ Easter Stories for Kids ~ Kids Read Along Books

summaries.summary: Little Cub loves Easter, so Papa Bear explains why it is special. Christmas celebrates Jesus’s birth, but Easter helps people remember that they can be with Jesus forever. Little Cub asks Papa Bear how God gave us Easter. Papa says Easter is part of God’s plan. An egg reminds them that Jesus was in a tomb but did not stay dead. Jesus is life, and God wants people to be with him always. During a walk, Little Cub and Papa see a fallen tree. The tree’s pine cones can make new trees, so Papa explains that new life can come after death. They also watch a river moving toward the ocean. The river ends, but it becomes part of something much bigger, like heaven. Papa tells Little Cub that God sent a flood with Noah and later gave a rainbow as a promise. When people disobeyed, Jesus kept the promise they broke, and God forgives people who believe in him. Little Cub listens with her heart and feels loved. The next morning, she says she heard, “I love you.”

Little Cub and Papa Bear talk about Easter while walking home. Little Cub likes the Easter Bunny and candy, but Papa explains that God is the one who gave Easter. Easter remembers Jesus, who was in a tomb but rose to life. Papa points to a fallen tree. Although it died, sunlight and pine cones help little trees grow. Then Papa compares a river to heaven: the river flows into the ocean, and people can become part of something bigger with God. He tells Little Cub about Noah, the flood, the rainbow promise, and how God wanted to stay close to his children. Jesus keeps the promise people broke and helps God forgive bad choices. Papa says he talks to Jesus all day and listens with his heart. Little Cub listens too. At bedtime, she feels cozy and cared for, as if Jesus whispers, “I love you.” The next morning, Papa calls those perfect Easter words.

video_title: 🎄 THE LITTLEST REINDEER Sometimes Little is the Perfect Size Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Dot was the littlest reindeer at the North Pole. She wanted to help fly Santa’s sleigh, so her sister Stina, her brother Oslo, and her grandpa taught her how to run, jump, and fly. Her friend Oliver reminded her that she could do many other things. Together, they built a snowman, played tag, made Christmas cards, and helped a baby fox find its mother. On Christmas Eve, a present fell from Santa’s bag. Dot ran after it and jumped as high as she could. She flew into Santa’s sleigh and returned with him. Everyone cheered. Dot lived with her reindeer family at Santa’s Village. She was the smallest reindeer, but she dreamed of flying Santa’s sleigh. Her sister showed her how to run, her brother showed her how to take off, and her grandpa showed her how to jump. Dot tried each lesson, but she could not run fast or jump high. A new harness even slipped off her. Dot became unhappy because she thought she could not help Santa. Then Oliver showed Dot that being small did not stop her from doing useful things. They made a snowman, played tag, created Christmas cards, and helped a lost baby fox. On Christmas Eve, Dot saw a present lying in the snow. She picked it up and ran beside the sleigh. When she jumped, she flew into it. Santa praised Dot, and the whole village celebrated her. Dot found a way to help after all.

At the North Pole, Dot was a little reindeer who wanted a special job. She hoped to fly with Santa, but learning was difficult. Stina taught her to get a running start, Oslo taught her to leap, and Grandpa taught her to jump from the stable loft. Dot tried with all her might, but she could not yet run, jump, or fly. Her mother told her there was always next year. Dot felt sad until Oliver helped her notice all the things she could already do. They played, made cards, and helped a baby fox return to its mother. Soon Christmas Eve came, and Santa’s reindeer began their journey. Dot noticed a present in the snow. She ran to get it and made her highest jump ever. This time, she flew into Santa’s sleigh. When they came home, everyone hugged and cheered. Dot learned that small can be just right.

video_title: 👹 Buffy the Vampire Slayer 👹 Stories for Kids Read Aloud [ READ ALONG VIDEO ]

When Buffy was eight years old, she believed a monster was hiding in her closet. At night, she heard sniffing, scratching, bumping, and thumping. Buffy was too scared to open the door, so she invited Willow and Xander to sleep over. They played games, ate popcorn, built pillow forts, and listened to music. The next day, they asked Giles, the librarian, for help. Giles explained that Buffy was a Slayer and could fight monsters when she was older. He told her to act brave, because acting brave would make the monster afraid. Buffy and her friends had another sleepover, but everyone still felt nervous. When the noises began, Buffy opened the closet. She and Willow went inside and discovered that the monsters were in a very small, uncomfortable space. The monsters had been noisy because the closet was crowded. Buffy felt sorry for them and invited them to join the sleepover.

Buffy tells how she became brave about the monster in her closet. At first, she was a young child who feared the dark. Her friends Willow and Xander stayed with her, but the strange noises continued after the lights went out. Buffy asked Giles for help at school. Giles said she was a Slayer and explained that she could face the monster by acting brave. Buffy and her friends planned another sleepover. They enjoyed games, popcorn, pillow forts, and music, but they were still nervous when the closet began to make noises. Buffy decided to open the door. She and Willow stepped into the dark closet and found the monsters. The monsters said they were sorry for making so much noise and explained that the closet was crowded. Buffy understood why they were noisy. She offered them water, tissues, and a blanket. The monsters became new guests, and everyone had the best sleepover ever.

video_title: The ABCs of Black History - An Animated Read Aloud with Moving Pictures

summaries.summary: The ABCs of Black history introduces important ideas, people, and celebrations from A to Z. A stands for an anthem that brings people together, while B celebrates beauty, bravery, and brotherhood. The poem explains how communities, churches, education, farming, family, freedom, and creativity have helped Black people survive and grow. It remembers the African diaspora, the Great Migration, Harlem, Juneteenth, Kwanzaa, marches, newspapers, voting, writers, and artists. It also names explorers, scientists, musicians, athletes, leaders, and queens. Harriet Tubman freed herself and helped free others. Martin Luther King Jr. dreamed of justice and encouraged people to keep marching. The poem says the struggle is not finished, but Black people remain unbroken, hopeful, powerful, and united. At Z, the highest point, the message is that the march toward freedom and victory continues, rising like the sun.

This alphabet poem teaches children about Black history through words, names, and events. It begins with hope and belonging in the anthem, then celebrates beautiful voices, brave people, strong families, and caring communities. It remembers Africans who were taken from their homes and carried across the ocean, but it also shows how people explored, learned, invented, created music, and built new communities. The poem tells about the Great Migration, Harlem’s artists, Juneteenth, and Kwanzaa. It honors marchers, organizers, newspapers, voters, writers, scientists, athletes, musicians, and queens. It explains that freedom and power are connected to courage, education, voting, and working together. Harriet Tubman, Reverend King, and many others helped move the fight forward. The poem ends with a mountain peak and a promise: even when some leaders cannot finish the journey, people will continue marching toward freedom, justice, hope, and victory.

From A to Z, the poem connects Black history with family, freedom, art, learning, and hope. It says that an anthem can help people feel that they belong. It praises Black beauty and remembers brave people who stood up when others told them to step back. It describes the African shore, the journey of the African diaspora, and the communities formed in new places. Children learn about education leaders and students who opened the doors of all-white schools. The poem celebrates food, folklore, farming, music, Harlem, imagination, Juneteenth, and Kwanzaa. It calls people to march, organize, vote, write, create, and use their power. It remembers leaders such as Harriet Tubman, Reverend King, and Shirley Chisholm, along with athletes, singers, scientists, and artists. The final letter, Z, stands for the highest peak. The journey is difficult, but the poem says people will keep rising and marching until victory is won.

video_title: I Promise | A story about being the Best you can be !

summaries.summary: The speaker makes many promises about becoming the best version of themselves. First, they promise to work hard, do what is right, go to school, read, follow rules, and respect the game plan. They promise to keep trying, get back up after mistakes, and be open to new things. This story is a joyful list of promises for growing and doing one’s best. The speaker begins by promising to work hard and make good choices. Fox and Hare were close friends with special senses. Fox could sniff far away things, while Hare could hear them. One day, Bird told them about winter and a thing called snow. They traveled through the forest to ask animals about it. Bear told them snow was white, Caribou told them snow was cold, Salmon told them snow was fluffy, and Goose told them snow was sparkly. Fox and Hare kept searching, but they did not find snow before night came. They slept near a lake with Hare’s thick tail around them. During the night, snowflakes quietly fell from the sky. When Fox and Hare woke, the world was white, cold, fluffy, and sparkly. They happily greeted the snow and played by tumbling and rolling in it. Bear and Caribou were glad to find them. Caribou led the friends home, while Fox remembered the path.

video_title: Ducks don't wear socks kids book read along

summaries.summary: Emily was a very serious girl who liked taking serious walks. She met Duck, who was playful and not serious. Emily asked about Duck’s socks, but Duck said ducks did not wear socks because he had cold feet. The next day, Duck wore a tie. Emily said ducks did not wear ties, but Duck had a big meeting. Then Duck wore a hat because he was late for the roundup. Emily tried not to laugh. The next day, Duck wore boots because he had fields to plow and crops to plant. Emily began to smile. Soon Duck wore underwear, and Emily said she had never seen a duck wearing underwear. Duck shouted about pants on the line and went away. Emily smiled, giggled, and laughed. At last, she met Duck again and asked what he was wearing. Duck laughed and said he was a duck. Emily and Duck laughed together and went off happily.

Emily always acted very seriously, but Duck kept making her smile. First, Emily saw Duck and asked about his socks. Duck said he did not wear socks and hurried away because he had cold feet. The next day, Duck wore a tie. Emily pointed out that ducks did not wear ties, while Duck said he had a big meeting. After that, Duck wore a hat because he was late for the roundup. Emily almost laughed. Then Duck came wearing boots. He said he had fields to plow and crops to plant, and Emily’s lips curled into a smile. The following day, Duck wore underwear. Emily had never seen a duck wearing underwear. Duck yelled about pants on the line and sailed away. Emily smiled, giggled, and laughed. Finally, she asked Duck what he was wearing. Duck laughed, “I’m a duck!” They laughed and went away together.

A serious girl named Emily met a silly duck named Duck. Emily noticed that Duck wore unusual things. When she asked about socks, Duck said he had cold feet and ran away. Later, Duck wore a tie and said he had a big meeting. Then he wore a hat and said he was late for the roundup. Emily tried hard to stay serious, but she almost laughed. The next day, Duck wore boots. He said he needed them to plow fields and plant crops. Emily started smiling. After that, Duck wore underwear. Emily said she had never seen a duck wear underwear. Duck called out about pants on the line and sailed away. Emily smiled, giggled, and laughed a little before bed. The next day, Emily asked Duck what he was wearing. Duck laughed and said he was a duck. Emily and Duck laughed so hard that they cried and quacked, then went off together.

video_title: The Princess and the Pizza- read aloud

summaries.summary: Princess Paulina lives in a small shack after her father gives up his throne to become a woodcarver. She misses being a princess, so she travels to Blom Castle when Queen Zelda announces a bride contest for Prince Drewpert. Paulina passes the mattress test and the glass-slipper test, even though she complains about the silly challenges. For the final test, the other princesses take nearly all the food, leaving Paulina only flour, yeast, water, tomatoes, and stale cheese. She mixes them together and falls asleep. When she learns the losers may be beheaded, she rushes to cook the messy mixture with garlic and herbs. It becomes a delicious pizza. Prince Drooper tastes it, and Paulina wins. She decides she does not want to marry him and opens a pizza palace instead. People love her pizzas and wave when she passes by.

Paulina used to be a princess, but now she lives in a humble shack with her father, who is learning to carve wood. She tries to act royal, but a chicken pecks her, the roof makes holes, and townspeople think her royal wave is a fly swat. Then she hears that Queen Zelda wants a true princess for Prince Drewpert. At the castle, Paulina must sleep on sixteen mattresses, wear glass slippers, and cook a feast. She succeeds at the first two tests. During the cooking test, other contestants leave her with only a few ingredients and no cooking tools. Her first dish looks terrible, so she naps. She wakes when the queen threatens the losers and quickly cooks the dish over hot coals. The cheese melts, the tomatoes bubble, and the garlic smells wonderful. Prince Drooper loves it, and Paulina’s pizza wins. She opens a busy pizza palace and becomes happy.

After losing her royal home, Princess Paulina wants a new job and hopes to become a princess again. She goes to Queen Zelda’s castle for a contest. First, Paulina proves she can feel a pea beneath many mattresses. Next, she tries on glass slippers and remains in the contest. For the last challenge, she must make a feast, but two other princesses and their helpers take almost everything. Paulina receives flour, yeast, water, tomatoes, and cheese. Without pots or spoons, she makes a flat, ugly mixture and decides to rest. When she hears that the losers will be beheaded, she adds garlic and herbs and places the tray near the fire. The mixture turns into pizza. Prince Drooper says it smells delicious, and the queen names Paulina’s pizza the winner. Paulina refuses to marry the prince and keeps her recipe secret. She opens a pizza restaurant with carved furniture, and everyone enjoys her food.

video_title: Everything You Need for a Treehouse | The guide to your own magical treehouse

summaries.summary: A tree house begins with time, looking up, and imagining a home high in a tree. The tree might stand alone or grow among many trees, but it should be tall enough to see sunlight. The builder needs blueprints, a hammer, nails, a saw, and a hard hat. Next come stilts, a ladder, a box for flowers, and places for begonias, zinnias, slugs, and marigolds. A swing, rope, and a way to climb make the tree house fun. A bookshelf, snacks, a sleeping bag, warm socks, pillows, and a flashlight make it cozy. Friends can share squeezed hands, secrets, and whispers while the wind keeps them safe. If a whisper breaks, they can yell, and animals will answer with sounds. Everything needed for a tree house includes time, looking up, flowers, snacks, friends, and imagination.

To make a tree house, first choose a tall tree and imagine a home of timber and rafters. The tree may be alone or part of a grove, with balconies, branches, or a turret-like top. Draw blueprints, gather a hammer, nails, a saw, and a hard hat, then build with slats, stilts, and a ladder. Add flower boxes and pickets for begonias and zinnias, and leave tiny gifts for slugs. A swing or rope helps you climb and move around. A bookshelf gives space for adventures, while a backpack holds treats such as red licorice, peaches, or pistachios. A hole-free sleeping bag, fuzzy socks, pillows, and a flashlight keep the high hideaway comfortable. Friends make it special by sharing secrets and holding hands as the wind rustles around them.

Everything for a tree house starts with time, looking up, and imagining. A tall tree lets someone see sun speckles and build a high hideaway. The builder makes blueprints and uses a hammer, nails, a saw, stilts, and a ladder. Flowers can grow in a box, and a swing or rope gives a way to climb, stretch, and slide. A bookshelf, snacks, a sleeping bag, warm socks, pillows, and a flashlight make the tree house ready for day and night. The builder may watch stars, make shadows, and listen to a bullfrog chorus. Friends can squeeze hands and share quiet secrets because the wind keeps whispers snug. If something makes a scary sound, they can warble or yell, and thrashers, barn owls, and crickets may answer. A tree house is made from building, nature, friendship, and imagination.

video_title: Everything You Need for a Treehouse | The guide to your own magical treehouse

summaries.summary: The brain in the poem loves learning and collecting facts. It takes in knowledge about spaceships, trains, planes, rain, grains, chains, and cranes. Sometimes thinking becomes hard, and the speaker feels frustrated or says they cannot think anymore. Then the speaker remembers to use the brain: they inhale and exhale, explain the feeling, and remind themselves that their big brain is helpful and wise. The brain becomes a friendly guide for learning and growing. The poem also says that brains do not all work in exactly the same way, but every brain is special and has a person inside it. His brain, her brain, their brain, and the speaker’s brain are all working just fine. At the end, the speaker thanks the brain for helping with training and showing that there is always more to learn and explain.

The speaker says, “I love my brain,” because it helps them stay sane and learn many things. Their brain gathers facts like a drain, including facts about spaceships and trains. A friend named Elaine says that her brain can be tough to maintain. The speaker understands this feeling too. Sometimes the speaker thinks they cannot think anymore, feels frustrated, or becomes confused. When that happens, the speaker pauses to inhale and exhale. Then they explain the strain and remember how much they love their big brain. Instead of hiding from difficult thoughts, they use the brain as a friendly guide. The speaker lists more things to learn, including planes, rain, grains, chains, and cranes. Finally, the poem explains that every person’s brain is special, even when brains work differently. The speaker thanks their brain for helping them learn and grow.

The poem celebrates a brain that learns, remembers, and helps with hard moments. The speaker’s brain gathers facts about many subjects, such as spaceships, trains, planes, rain, grains, chains, and cranes. Elaine says that keeping her brain working can be difficult, and the speaker admits feeling that way sometimes. When thoughts become frustrating or difficult to contain, the speaker may feel like complaining or become confused. Then the speaker uses the brain by breathing in and out, naming the strain, and remembering that the brain is helpful and wise. The speaker lets the big brain guide the way and enjoys having more facts to learn. The poem also honors all kinds of brains. Some brains may not work exactly alike, but every brain is special, and every person inside a brain matters. The speaker ends by thanking and loving their brain.

video_title: 'Just for You' Read By Hannah Gordon | Halloween Short Stories

summaries.summary: Rosie Gray, a famous actress, moves with her agent Sheila to an isolated house in the Lake District. Rosie is frightened because a killer has murdered nine women and seems to be acting in her name. The killer has called her repeatedly, whispering, “Just for you.” Rosie hopes her boyfriend, Ritchie, will make her feel safer. When Ritchie arrives, he tells Sheila that another woman has been murdered. During a violent storm, the electricity fails, and a telephone rings inside a drinks cabinet, although the house has no phone. Someone then knocks heavily at the front door and walks around the house. Rosie and Sheila cannot find the portable phone. Sergeant Cooper arrives, warning that another murder has happened nearby and that the killer may be close. He takes Rosie outside. Sheila hears glass breaking upstairs and collapses when someone grabs her. Ritchie later breaks in through a window and reveals that no police officer has been checking the house. Then the hidden phone rings again.

Rosie Gray leaves London for a lonely country house after a murderer begins killing women as supposed sacrifices to her. The killer phones Rosie and whispers, “Just for you,” making her terrified of every sound. Sheila, her agent, tries to protect her and tells her that Ritchie, Rosie’s younger boyfriend, is coming. Ritchie arrives with news of another ritualistic murder, but Sheila keeps it from Rosie because she is already nervous. That night, a storm causes the lights to go out. A telephone rings in the dark, even though Sheila insists they have no telephone. When the lights return, they discover a portable phone hidden among bottles in a drinks cabinet. Soon someone knocks violently, then moves around the outside of the house. Sheila and Rosie search for the phone but cannot find it. Sergeant Cooper appears and leads Rosie away, saying a murder occurred nearby. Sheila hears a window break upstairs and is attacked. Ritchie finally enters and says the police were never there. The phone begins ringing again.

Rosie and Sheila settle into a large, isolated house near Lake Ullswater, hoping its distance from London will protect Rosie from a dangerous murderer. The killer has murdered nine women and calls Rosie every night, saying the killings are “just for you.” Rosie is still grieving and frightened, while Sheila works hard to keep her calm. Ritchie visits after another woman is found with the same ritualistic injuries. Sheila does not tell Rosie about this new murder. That evening, a storm darkens the house. During the blackout, a telephone rings from somewhere nearby. The women discover a portable phone concealed in the drinks cabinet, although neither of them brought it. A figure approaches the house, and loud knocks shake the front door. Sheila searches for the phone while Rosie fears the killer has arrived. Sergeant Cooper suddenly comes to rescue them and says another murder has taken place down the valley. Rosie leaves with him, but Sheila remains behind. A window shatters upstairs, and an unseen person rushes toward Sheila. Ritchie later breaks in and says there had been no police protection. The phone rings once more.

video_title: Appa Reads: The Yellow Bus by Loren Long

summaries.summary: A bright yellow bus spent her days driving. Every morning, people climbed inside with pitterpatters and giggles. She carried them from one important place to another, and their happy sounds filled her with joy. Then a new driver took her along unfamiliar roads. Later, another driver left her in a quiet place in the city and never came back. Nobody climbed in, and the bus became empty and quiet. One cold night, some people came inside and huddled together. They returned every night with soft voices, making the bus happy again. A truck carried her across the city and countryside to a farm beside a river. Animals climbed in with clip-clops, but the farmer later took them away. The river rose, and soon swimmers came into the bus. They drifted around her, and even though she carried nobody anywhere, they filled her with joy.

The yellow bus loved carrying people. Each morning, they climbed aboard, making sounds like pitterpatter and giggles. The bus took them to important places, and she felt joyful. Then drivers changed. One driver left the bus in the city, where nobody came inside. She missed the footsteps, laughter, shuffles, and clunks. On a cold night, people came to stay warm and huddled together. They came back every night, so the bus was happy again. One morning, a truck moved the bus far away to a farm in a valley beside a river. Some animals climbed inside and made clip-clop sounds. Soon, the farmer gathered the animals and took them away, leaving the farm and bus quiet. Then the river rose higher and higher. The yellow bus was alone until swimmers came into her. They moved all around her, and the bus felt joy again, even though she did not carry them from place to place.

A yellow bus had many busy days. People climbed in every morning, and she carried them from one important place to another. Their footsteps, giggles, and other sounds made her happy. After some time, a driver left her alone in the city. No one climbed in, and the bus heard no happy sounds. On a cold night, people came inside and huddled together. They returned every night and filled her with joy. Then a truck towed the bus through the city and countryside to a farm near a river. Animals climbed into her and made clip-clop noises, but the farmer soon took them away. The farm became quiet. The river then began to swell and rise. The yellow bus was alone until swimmers came into her. They swam in and out and all around the bus. She did not take them anywhere, but their movement filled her with joy.

video_title: Toy Story 4@Readingtimewithnana

summaries.summary: Woody loved Andy and led the toys. Later, Woody belonged to Bonnie. Bonnie made Forky from a spork and art supplies, but Forky did not know he was a toy. When Forky ran away during a trip, Woody followed him because he would not leave a toy behind. Woody met Bo Peep again, and Buzz met Ducky and Bunny. Together, the toys tried to rescue Forky from an antique store. Gabby Gabby wanted Woody’s voice box, so Woody gave it to her. Then the toys helped Gabby Gabby find a child. A lost girl hugged Gabby Gabby, and Gabby Gabby found a kid. Bonnie was happy to see Forky. Woody was happy too. He stayed with Bo Peep and his friends because he wanted to help toys who were lost and lonely.

Bonnie made a new toy named Forky, but Forky thought he was only a spork. He ran away from Bonnie’s family, so Woody chased after him and promised to bring him back. Woody and Forky went to an antique store and met Gabby Gabby, who wanted Woody’s voice box. Woody escaped and found Bo Peep. Buzz, Ducky, Bunny, and Duke Kaboom joined them. The toys tried to save Forky, but Forky was still trapped. Woody made a deal with Gabby Gabby. He gave her his voice box so she could go to Bonnie and find a child. The toys rode high at the carnival and used Duke’s motorcycle to cross the crowd. Gabby Gabby saw a lost girl. The girl hugged her and then found her parents. Gabby Gabby now had a kid. Forky returned to Bonnie, and Woody stayed with his toy friends to help others.

Woody was a sheriff toy who cared for his children and his friends. He helped Bonnie make Forky, but Forky ran away because he did not think he was a toy. Woody followed him to a town and an antique store. There, Forky was captured, and Woody met Gabby Gabby. Bo Peep helped Woody, while Buzz, Ducky, Bunny, and Duke Kaboom helped too. The toys escaped the store, but Forky was left behind. Woody went back and traded his voice box to Gabby Gabby for Forky. At the carnival, the toys found a way to reach Bonnie. Duke Kaboom rode his motorcycle over the crowd, carrying the toys on a string. Gabby Gabby found a lost girl who needed a friend. The girl hugged Gabby Gabby, so Gabby Gabby became her toy. Bonnie was delighted to see Forky. Woody then chose to help lost toys with Bo Peep and their friends.

video_title: Commotion in the Ocean 🐙🪼 | Fun Kids Book Read Aloud | Sea Animal Storytime for Children

summaries.summary: At the bottom of the ocean, many creatures are swimming and hiding among the rocks. A crab walks sideways and pretends to be a spy. Turtles crawl onto the beach, lay eggs, and watch the babies hurry across the sand. Dolphins speak with clicks, whistles, and squeaks. An angel fish thinks she is very pretty, while a jellyfish likes to jiggle. A shark opens its wide jaws, and a swordfish chases little fish. An octopus uses eight arms to hold and tickle its children. A stingray has a stinging tail, and a lobster can pinch fingers. Far below, strange fish have teeth, big eyes, fins, and glowing whiskers. A giant blue whale is very long. Barnacles cling, walruses bellow, penguins slide and splash, and a mother polar bear cuddles her children. The dolphin is friendly, but the shark is most dangerous.

The ocean is full of swimming creatures, so we look closely between the rocks to find them. The crab moves sideways to look sneaky. Turtles come from the water to bury many eggs on the dry beach, and the babies scamper through the sand when they hatch. Dolphins do not say ordinary words; they make clicking, whistling, and squeaking sounds. The angel fish says she is beautiful, and the jellyfish happily jiggles. A shark grins and opens its jaws. A swordfish chases small fish and catches some when it is hungry. An octopus has eight arms to hold and tickle its children. The stingray flaps its wings but has a tail that stings. A lobster snaps its claws. Deep underwater, unusual fish have big teeth, huge eyes, fins, and glowing whiskers. A whale is enormous. Penguins splash, and a polar bear hugs her children. The shark is the most dangerous.

A curious commotion is happening under the sea. We meet crabs, turtles, dolphins, fish, sharks, an octopus, a stingray, a lobster, a whale, barnacles, walruses, penguins, and a polar bear. The crab walks sideways like a spy. Turtles lay eggs on the beach, and their babies run over the sand. Dolphins make little clicks, whistles, and squeaks. The angel fish admires her beauty, while the jellyfish has fun jiggling. The shark invites someone to look inside its wide mouth, but it is dangerous. The swordfish catches fish with its sword. The octopus uses its arms to hold and tickle its children. The stingray can sting, and the lobster can snip fingers. Strange deep-sea fish have glowing whiskers. The blue whale is huge, barnacles cling to things, and walruses bellow. Penguins slide and splash in the water. In the cold Arctic, a mother polar bear cuddles her children.

video_title: 👻Spooky Old Tree, by Stan and Jan Berenstain, Children’s Story, Read Aloud, Berenstain Bears

summaries.summary: Three little bears go into a spooky old tree. One bear has a light, one has a stick, and one has a rope. They see a twisty old stair and decide to go up it. Then they find a giant key and a moving wall. They are brave and go through the wall into a spooky old hall. In the hall, there is a great sleeping bear. By then, one bear has the light, but two bears have the shivers. Still, they go over the sleeping bear because they already came into the tree, climbed the stair, went through the wall, and entered the hall. Soon, all three bears have the shivers. They do not have the light, stick, or rope anymore. They find a way out by going up a ladder, through the floor, down a slide, and out a door. Then they run home, safe at last.

Three little bears wonder if they dare enter a spooky old tree. One carries a light, one carries a stick, and one carries a rope. They say yes and go inside. Next, they find a twisty old stair and climb up. They also find a giant key and a wall that moves. The bears dare to go through the wall and enter a spooky old hall. There they see a great sleeping bear. One bear still has the light, but two bears have the shivers. The bears go over the sleeping bear and continue on. Now they are all shivering, and they have no light, stick, or rope. They need to get out. They go up a ladder, through the floor, down a slide, and out a door. Then the three little bears run fast and get home safely.

The story follows three little bears on a scary adventure. They enter a spooky old tree. At first, they have useful things: a light, a stick, and a rope. They climb a twisty old stair. Then they find a giant key and a moving wall. The bears go through the wall and into a spooky old hall. A great sleeping bear is there. The bears have already come so far, so they go over the sleeping bear too. During the adventure, the light, stick, and rope are gone, and all three bears have the shivers. They wonder how they will ever get out. Then they find a way. They go up a ladder, through the floor, down a slide, and out a door. The three little bears run fast and return home safe at last.

video_title: With My Daddy - A Book of Love & Family

summaries.summary: A child loves being with Dad. The child hugs Dad and feels safe in his warm arms. Nothing seems scary—not darkness, monsters, or the neighbor’s dog—because the child feels brave with Dad nearby. Dad lifts, twirls, and tosses the child like a rocket. He helps the child ride a bike and cheers at the finish line, so the child feels confident. At the pool, they play like a boat and a pirate. They also pretend to fly to the moon and play many games together. On a warm day, they rest and listen to the wind. Sometimes the child feels excited or angry. Dad plays the monster, then stops when the child says, “That’s enough.” He hugs the child until the storm of anger passes. At bedtime, Dad carries the child upstairs, gives a kiss, and says good night. The child knows they love each other.

With Dad, an ordinary day becomes full of safe and happy adventures. The child hugs Dad and feels like a little bird in a cozy nest. Dad helps the child feel brave when scary things are imagined, and he lifts the child high like a rocket. When the child wobbles on a bike, Dad pushes gently, cheers, and believes in the child. The child then believes in themself and crosses the finish line. At the pool, Dad pretends to be a boat while the child plays a fierce pirate. They imagine riding a flying carpet to the moon and becoming astronauts, acrobats, and lion tamers. The child can also feel calm, excited, or angry. When anger grows like a storm, Dad holds the child and says, “Stop. That’s enough.” The child becomes peaceful again. At night, Dad tucks the child into bed. They hug, say good night, and remember their love.

The child shares many feelings that come from time spent with Dad. A hug makes the child feel safe, and Dad’s presence makes dark things, monsters, and barking dogs seem less frightening. Dad lifts and twirls the child, making the child feel daring. He encourages the child on a bicycle and celebrates at the finish line, helping the child feel confident. Together they swim, pretend to sail, fly to the moon, and play special games for two. They rest in the yard and feel calm while the wind blows. Sometimes the child becomes excited and runs from a pretend arm monster. Sometimes the child becomes angry, rolling and crying as feelings grow like thunder and rain. Dad stops the game, hugs tightly, and rubs the child’s back until the storm passes. Later, Dad carries the child to bed, gives a kiss, and says good night. The child loves Dad, and Dad loves the child.

video_title: 👧🏻 The Gingerbread Girl

summaries.summary: A lonely old woman and old man made a gingerbread girl after a fox caught their gingerbread boy. The girl woke up in the oven and ran away. She met farmers, a pig, an artist, a cow, three dogs, children, and teachers. Everyone chased her, but she sang that she was too fast to catch. At the river, the same fox offered to help her cross. The gingerbread girl carefully climbed onto his tail. When the fox swam into deep water, she moved to his head, tied his snout with her licorice hair, and made him turn around. She rode the fox back to the house while the crowd followed. Then she and the old couple made more gingerbread. The house was happy and no longer lonely. The gingerbread girl also taught the fox some manners with gingerbread crumbs.

After losing their gingerbread boy, a lonely old woman and man baked a sweet gingerbread girl. As soon as the oven opened, she jumped out and ran down the path. Farmers chased her, but she was faster. A pig tried to bite her, an artist tried to catch her, and a cow, dogs, schoolchildren, and teachers joined the chase. The gingerbread girl kept running and singing. At the river, a sly fox promised to carry her safely. She climbed onto his tail, but the fox planned to eat her. When he told her to move to his head, she pulled off a licorice strand, tied the fox's snout, and turned him around. She rode him home. Everyone followed, and the old couple helped make more gingerbread. The home became happy, and the girl taught the fox good manners.

The gingerbread girl was made to bring happiness back to a lonely old woman and old man. She was covered with candies and had licorice hair. But when she came out of the oven, she ran away. Many hungry people and animals chased her, including farmers, a pig, an artist, a cow, three dogs, children, and teachers. The gingerbread girl was quick and escaped them all. Then she reached the river where a devious fox was waiting. He said he would help her cross, but he wanted to eat her. The clever girl let him carry her into the water. When the fox told her to climb to his head, she tied his snout with her licorice hair. She made him turn back and rode him to the house. The crowd came too. The old couple made more gingerbread, and their home was happy. The girl later taught the fox manners.

video_title: Peppa Pig, Peppa‘s first sleepover. Children’s bedtime story read aloud in an English accent.

summaries.summary: Peppa goes to Zoe Zebra’s house for her first sleepover. Rebecca Rabbit, Suzy Sheep, and Emily Elephant are there too. Each girl brings a special toy. Zoe’s baby twin sisters, Zuzu and Zaza, want to join them. Zoe says sleepovers are for big girls, but the twins cry, so the girls let them stay. The friends play the piano, but Mommy Zebra asks them to be quiet because Daddy Zebra must sleep. The girls get into their sleeping bags and plan a midnight feast. They quietly go to the kitchen and take fruit. The floor creaks, and Mommy Zebra wakes up. The girls tell a story about a fairy and a monster, but Emily makes a loud elephant noise. Daddy Zebra wakes up too. He finishes the story by singing quietly about a little star. His gentle song makes everyone fall asleep.

Peppa has her first sleepover at Zoe Zebra’s house. Rebecca, Suzy, and Emily come with their favorite toys, and Zoe welcomes them. Zuzu and Zaza, Zoe’s baby sisters, want to join. At first, Zoe says they are too little, but the twins cry, so they may stay if they do not fall asleep. The girls play “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” on the piano. Mommy Zebra tells them to be quiet because Daddy Zebra is sleeping. Soon the girls want a midnight feast. They sneak to the kitchen and collect delicious fruit. The floorboards creak, and Mommy Zebra wakes up. The girls begin a bedtime story about a fairy and a monster. Emily makes a loud trumpeting sound, which wakes Daddy Zebra. Daddy Zebra joins the story and sings quietly while playing the piano. His song sends all the girls to sleep.

At Zoe Zebra’s house, Peppa enjoys her very first sleepover with Rebecca Rabbit, Suzy Sheep, and Emily Elephant. The girls bring a teddy, a carrot, an owl, a frog, and Zoe’s monkey. Zoe’s baby twins, Zuzu and Zaza, cry because they want to stay. The girls let them join. First, Zoe plays the piano, but Mommy Zebra says everyone must be quiet so Daddy Zebra can sleep. The friends climb into their sleeping bags and decide to have a secret midnight feast. They go to the kitchen and pick fruit, but the floor creaks. Mommy Zebra wakes up and asks for a bedtime story. The girls tell a fairy story about a big monster. Emily makes an elephant noise, and Daddy Zebra wakes up. He tells what the monster did and sings “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” softly. The song makes everyone go to sleep.

video_title: Planes Read Along Story book, Read Aloud Story Books, Planes - Dusty Flies High

summaries.summary: Dusty is a crop-dusting plane who dreams of becoming a great racer. His friend Chug helps him, and Dottie fixes planes, but she tells Dusty that he is not meant to race. Dusty tries anyway and does well, so he joins the around-the-world race. During the race, flying high makes him sick, and flying low nearly sends him into an iceberg. When another plane gets oil in its eyes, Dusty slows down and helps it land safely. Dusty removes his heavy crop-dusting gear and flies faster, but Ripslinger wants to be the only winner. After Dusty’s antenna is broken, he gets lost, and the jets and pitties repair and refuel him. Dusty later crashes into the ocean during a storm. His friends share their parts, Dottie fixes him, and he returns to the race. Dusty flies high, passes Ripslinger, and wins. His friends cheer because his dream has come true.

Dusty wants to race even though Dottie says he is not meant to. With help from Chug and Dottie, he enters the around-the-world race. At first, Dusty flies fast through the turns and does well. He has trouble when flying high makes him sick, and he nearly hits an iceberg while flying low. Dusty also sees another plane that cannot see because of oil in its eyes. He slows down and helps the plane land safely. Dusty takes off his heavy crop-dusting gear and becomes faster, making him a fan favorite. Ripslinger is angry and wants to win alone. Dusty gets lost after his antenna is broken, but the jets and pitties fix and refuel him. A storm makes Dusty crash into the ocean. His friends share their parts, Dottie repairs him, and Dusty returns. He flies high, passes Ripslinger, and wins the race.

Dusty begins as a crop-dusting plane who wishes to become a racer. Dottie warns him that he is not meant to race, but Dusty enters the big around-the-world race anyway. He flies fast and becomes a fan favorite after removing his heavy crop-dusting gear. Dusty helps another plane land when oil covers its eyes, but Ripslinger does not like Dusty and wants to be the only winner. Ripslinger’s friend breaks Dusty’s antenna, and Dusty becomes lost over the ocean. He lands on a ship, where the jets and pitties fix and refuel him. Later, Dusty flies into a storm and crashes into the ocean. A helicopter pulls him out, but his broken parts keep him from finishing. The other racers visit and share their parts. Dottie fixes Dusty, and he rejoins the race. Dusty flies high through the clouds, passes Ripslinger, wins, and hears his friends cheer.

video_title: Body Boundaries Make Me Stronger | Read Aloud by Reading Pioneers Academy

summaries.summary: Nick enjoys playing on the playground until Ben tickles and pokes him too much. Nick does not like those touches, so he goes home and tells his parents how he feels. His mother explains that Nick owns his body and may say no to hugs, kisses, tickles, or any other touch he does not want. She teaches him that everyone has a personal space, like an invisible bubble, and that private parts must stay covered. Nick learns to tell his safety team if anyone makes him uncomfortable or offers treats for touching him. His safety team can include parents, teachers, grandparents, or an older brother. When Auntie visits, Nick asks for a high five instead of hugs and kisses, and she respects his choice. Nick also learns to ask permission before touching other people. He refuses unpleasant touches but enjoys his mother’s gentle caress and goodnight kiss.

At the playground, Ben keeps tickling and poking Nick. Nick feels uncomfortable and leaves with his toys. At home, Nick’s mother notices that he is upset. Nick tells both parents the truth. He says that Ben’s touching feels bad, and that Auntie’s very strong hugs and endless kisses can also be unwelcome. His mother says Nick can refuse touches kindly because his body belongs to him. She explains that personal space is like an invisible bubble. No one may touch or look at the private parts under his underwear, except that a doctor may check his body with a parent present. Nick learns that a safety team is made of trusted adults who can help him. If they are not nearby, he should tell another adult or leave. Nick feels safer and speaks up. When Auntie arrives, he chooses a high five. He remembers to respect other people’s boundaries too.

Nick learns an important lesson about body boundaries. First, he discovers that tickling and poking can stop being fun when someone does not want them. He tells his parents, and they listen carefully. They explain that nice touches are not always welcome, and Nick can say no with kind words. He may choose a high five or a handshake instead of a hug or kiss. His parents also teach him to protect his personal space and private parts. A doctor may help care for him during a checkup when his parent is with him, but nobody else should touch or see his private parts. If someone offers candy or sweets for touching, Nick should know it is a trap and tell his safety team. Later, Nick asks Auntie for a high five, and she agrees. Nick feels safe, learns to speak up, and treats others with the same respect.

video_title: THE THREE PIGS Read by Mrs. K | Written by David Wiesner | Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Three pigs leave home to seek their fortunes. The first pig builds a straw house, but a wolf huffs and puffs it down and eats the pig. The second pig builds a house of sticks, and the wolf blows it down too. The two pigs escape from the story and meet their brother, the third pig. They explore a nursery rhyme and see a cat, a cow, a dog, a dish, and a spoon. Then they visit a story about a dragon guarding a golden rose. A brave prince defeats the dragon, and the pigs invite the dragon to come with them. The pigs return to their brick house and discover that the wolf cannot blow it down. The wolf comes inside, and everyone has soup. The pigs, the dragon, and their friends stay together and live happily ever after.

In the story, three pigs build different houses. The first pig chooses straw, and the second chooses sticks. A wolf visits both houses and blows them down after saying, “I’ll huff and I’ll puff.” The pigs escape from the pages instead of staying in the wolf’s story. They find another story with the words “Hey diddle diddle,” where a cat plays a fiddle, a cow jumps over the moon, a dog laughs, and a dish runs away with a spoon. Next, they enter a dragon tale. A prince rides to the mountaintop, defeats a great dragon, and rescues him from the story. The pigs and the dragon become friends. Finally, they return to the brick house. The wolf tries to blow it down, but he cannot. Everyone comes inside for soup, and they all live happily ever after.

The three pigs begin by building houses so they can seek their fortunes. A straw house and a stick house do not protect the first two pigs from the wolf. After the wolf blows those houses down, the pigs step out of the story and explore other pages. They find a nursery rhyme and meet its cat, cow, little dog, dish, and spoon. Then they enter a tale about a golden rose and a dragon. A prince comes to the mountaintop, uses his sword to defeat the dragon, and rescues him. The pigs ask the dragon to travel with them. They find a castle made with brickwork and decide to go home. Back at the brick house, the wolf knocks and threatens to blow it down. He huffs and puffs, but the strong brick house stays standing. The pigs bring everyone inside, serve soup, and live happily ever after.

video_title: Little Bunny's Perfect Day! - A Counting Story - Read Aloud Kids Book - A Bedtime Story with Dessi!

summaries.summary: Little Bunny asks Mummy if he may play outside. Mummy says yes, but tells him to stay in the garden. Bunny goes out and meets a duckling. Then Bunny and the duckling meet a hedgehog, a frog, a kitten, a snail, a squirrel, a bee, a puppy, and a butterfly. Each friend joins the game, so the group grows from one friend to ten little friends. They play together on a sunny day. They play hide-and-seek, then tag. They also have a talent show, and everyone smiles while showing special talents. When the sun begins to set, the friends see the moon and decide to meet again soon. Bunny hops home happily. He made many friends and had a perfect day.

One little bunny goes outside to play after Mummy says he can stay in the garden. Along the way, Bunny invites a duckling to play. Soon, a hedgehog joins them. Then they meet a leaping frog, a kitten under a tree, and a slow snail. A squirrel, a bee, a puppy, and a butterfly join too. Now there are ten little friends. The friends have a happy day in the sunshine. They play hide-and-seek and tag. They laugh and enjoy a talent show where everyone shares a special skill. As evening comes and the sun goes down, the friends look at the moon. They plan to meet again soon. Bunny hops home with a big smile because he found lots of friends and enjoyed his perfect day.

Mummy lets Little Bunny play, as long as he does not go far from the garden. Bunny meets many animals and kindly asks each one to join him. First comes a yellow duckling. Then come a hedgehog, a frog, a kitten, a snail, a squirrel, a bee, a puppy, and a butterfly. The friends play together until there are ten of them. They have fun on a lovely sunny day. They play hide-and-seek, chase one another in tag, and put on a talent show. Everyone smiles while showing what they can do. Later, the sun sets and the moon appears. The ten friends decide to play together again soon. Little Bunny goes home, hopping and smiling. He is happy because he spent the day making friends and having fun.

video_title: Chapter Book Storytime • 𝑇ℎ𝑒 𝑀𝑎𝑔𝑖𝑐 𝑀𝑖𝑠𝑓𝑖𝑡𝑠 • EVPL Digital Program

summaries.summary: Carter Locke is a young street magician running through a foggy train yard while a cruel man chases him. Carter reaches a moving train, escapes the man, and falls asleep inside a freight car with his satchel under his head. While he sleeps, the story goes back to explain his past. Carter once lived happily with his parents, who were skilled at magic tricks, but they disappeared and never came home. He was taken in by his unpleasant uncle, Sylvester Sly. Uncle Sly taught Carter many tricks, and Carter quickly became very talented. On Carter’s birthday, Uncle Sly sent him to perform for a couple. Carter amazed them by making a card disappear, finding another card in the man’s pocket, and producing paper flowers. The couple applauded and gave Carter a nickel. Carter felt proud because he had made them happy. Later, however, he discovered that Uncle Sly had secretly stolen the man’s watch and the woman’s wedding ring. Carter realized that his uncle had used him to rob innocent people, and his happiness disappeared.

The story begins with Carter Locke fleeing across a dark train yard. A man follows him and threatens to hurt him, so Carter races beside a colorful moving train. The train reminds him of the first magic trick he saw from his father, involving scarves pulled from an ear. Carter tries to jump onto a yellow train car, but the man grabs his satchel and pulls him down. Carter keeps moving, takes back his bag, and catches the ladder on the last car. He climbs onto the roof and watches the angry man shrink into the distance. Carter then rests inside the train and dreams about adventure and magic. The story flashes back to Carter’s childhood. His parents vanished, and Carter went to live with Uncle Sly, a dishonest man who taught him magic tricks. Carter became an excellent performer. During his first public show, he delighted a couple, but Uncle Sly secretly stole their valuables. Carter felt betrayed because his uncle had turned his talent into a tool for stealing.

Carter does not believe in real magic, but he is very skilled at performing tricks. At the start, he is escaping from a dangerous man in a train yard. Carter carefully chooses a train car, struggles with his pursuer, and finally climbs onto the back of the moving train. After the train carries him away, he sleeps among boxes. The story then explains why Carter was alone. His parents had been kind and talented, but they disappeared when he was small. His new guardian, Uncle Sly, was selfish and dishonest. Uncle Sly taught Carter tricks because he wanted a useful assistant. Carter learned quickly and could shuffle cards, vanish coins, and create cards from thin air. On his birthday, Carter performed for a couple and made them laugh and applaud. The man gave him a nickel, and Carter felt that he had brought happiness to them. Then Carter learned that Uncle Sly had stolen the couple’s watch and wedding ring. This ruined Carter’s good feeling and showed him that his uncle had misused his magic.

video_title: Panda Bear, Panda Bear, What Do You See? (My First Reader) Read Aloud Kids Book

summaries.summary: A panda bear is asked, “What do you see?” The panda bear sees a bald eagle soaring by. The bald eagle sees a water buffalo charging by. The water buffalo sees a spider monkey swinging by. The spider monkey sees a green sea turtle swimming by. The green sea turtle sees a Macaroni penguin starting by. The Macaroni penguin sees a sea lion splashing by. Then a red wolf is sneaking by, a whooping crane is flying by, and a black panther is strolling by. At the end, a dreaming child is watching over the wild animals. The animals are named again: the bald eagle, water buffalo, spider monkey, green sea turtle, Macaroni penguin, sea lion, red wolf, whooping crane, and black panther. They are all wild and free.

The story begins with a panda bear and a question: “What do you see?” One animal answers about another. First, the panda bear sees a bald eagle. The bald eagle sees a water buffalo. The water buffalo sees a spider monkey, and the spider monkey sees a green sea turtle. Next, the green sea turtle sees a Macaroni penguin. The Macaroni penguin sees a sea lion splashing. A red wolf sneaks by, a whooping crane flies by, and a black panther strolls by. The black panther sees a dreaming child watching over everything. At the end, the story names all the animals together. There is a bald eagle, a water buffalo, a spider monkey, a green sea turtle, a Macaroni penguin, a sea lion, a red wolf, a whooping crane, and a black panther. They are all wild and free.

A panda bear looks and sees a bald eagle soaring by. The bald eagle looks and sees a water buffalo charging. The water buffalo looks and sees a spider monkey swinging. The spider monkey looks and sees a green sea turtle swimming. The green sea turtle looks and sees a Macaroni penguin starting by. The Macaroni penguin looks and sees a sea lion splashing. Then a red wolf sneaks by. A whooping crane flies by. After that, a black panther strolls by. The black panther looks and sees a dreaming child watching over the animals. The story ends by naming the animals in order: bald eagle, water buffalo, spider monkey, green sea turtle, Macaroni penguin, sea lion, red wolf, whooping crane, and black panther. They are all wild and free, and that is what is seen.

video_title: Look Who's Here! 👀 Just for You Just for Me by Catherine Lukas  📖Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: A doorbell rings, and Tom is happy because his friend Clyde has arrived. Tom says Clyde is right on time and has come to play. Clyde makes beep, click, and clack sounds. He wants to play outside, so he tries the slide. But Clyde accidentally eats the slide and says he is sorry. More beep, click, and clack sounds follow. Clyde says he will come back soon, and then his ride arrives to take him home.

Tom welcomes Clyde when the doorbell rings. Tom is excited because Clyde is his new friend and has come to play. Clyde makes funny beep, click, and clack sounds. He would like to play outside. Clyde tries the slide, but he accidentally eats it. Clyde is sorry. Soon, Clyde says he will come back. Then his ride comes, and Clyde leaves. Tom and Clyde have shared a short playtime together.

The doorbell chimes, and Clyde arrives at Tom’s home. Tom says Clyde is on time and is ready to play. Clyde makes beep, click, and clack sounds. He wants to play outside. While playing, Clyde eats the slide by mistake. He says he is sorry. After more sounds, Clyde says he will come back soon. Then his ride arrives. Clyde goes away, but he plans to return another time.

video_title: THE BIGGEST SNOWMAN EVER | A Winter Read Aloud Picture Book | Storytime

summaries.summary: The mayor of Mouseville announces a contest: the mouse who builds the biggest snowman will win a prize. Clayton, a house mouse, and Desmond, a field mouse, each say that he will win. They build snowballs in different places and use wheelbarrows to carry snow faster. Soon, they notice that their snowmen are the same size as the other snow people in town. Clayton and Desmond each have an idea. They meet, bump into each other, and decide to work together. They roll all the snowman pieces into the middle of the field. Clayton adds a floppy hat, and Desmond adds a scarf, coal eyes, and a carrot nose. Their snowman becomes the biggest one ever. At the contest, the mayor gives both mice the prize because they built it together. Everyone celebrates with dancing, hot chocolate, and donuts.

Mouseville is covered with snow, and the mayor announces a snowman contest. Clayton and Desmond both want to make the biggest snowman ever. Each mouse starts building alone. Clayton rolls snow to make a base, belly, and head. Desmond does the same nearby. Their dad and uncle give them the same helpful advice: use a wheelbarrow to move the snow faster. After several days, Desmond sees the other snow creations and notices they are all the same size. Clayton notices this too. Then Clayton and Desmond walk toward each other with an idea. They fall when they bump together, but they decide to join their work. They roll both snowmen into one place and stack all the snowballs together. They decorate the giant snowman with a hat, scarf, coal eyes, and carrot nose. The judges arrive, and the mayor says both mice win. The friends celebrate together.

A winter snowstorm gives the mice of Mouseville plenty of snow for a contest. The mayor says the biggest snowman will win a prize. Clayton proudly says he will build it, but Desmond says he will build it instead. They work separately, rolling snow into large pieces. Their families help them by suggesting wheelbarrows.
