video_title: No, David!

summaries.summary: David's mom keeps saying, “No, David!” David reaches for cookies, brings mud inside, and splashes water out of the tub. He bangs on pans, plays with his food, and puts too much food in his mouth. His mom tells him to be quiet, stop, settle down, and go to his room. David pretends to be a superhero, picks his nose, and leaves many toys out. Then he tries to play baseball inside with a bat. The baseball breaks a vase, so David goes to timeout. His mom calls him to come close. Even after all the trouble, she tells David that she loves him. David's actions cause many problems, but his mom still loves him at the end of the story.

David has many busy adventures at home. First, he reaches for cookies while his mom says no. He walks with muddy feet, splashes water from the tub, and bangs on the pans. At mealtime, he plays with chicken legs, green beans, and a baked potato. He puts too much food in his mouth, so his mom sends him to his room. David then acts like a superhero, picks his nose, and leaves his toys everywhere. His mom says the toys cannot stay in the house. David also plays baseball indoors and hits the ball with a bat. The ball breaks a vase, and David must sit in timeout. Then his mom calls him, and she says, “Yes, David, I love you.”

David's day is full of things his mother does not want him to do. He reaches for cookies and tracks mud on his feet. In the bathtub, he gets wild and splashes water everywhere. He makes noise by banging on pans and plays with his food. After putting too much food in his mouth, he is told to go to his room. David settles down for a moment, but then he pretends to be a superhero, picks his nose, and leaves his toys out. He is told not to play baseball in the house. David hits the ball with a bat, and it breaks a vase. He goes to timeout. At the end, his mother calls him over and tells him she loves him.

video_title: Pete The Cat And His Magic Sunglasses- Read Along, Kids book

summaries.summary: Pete the cat felt unhappy and had the blue cat blues. Grumpy Toad gave him cool blue magic sunglasses. Pete put them on and noticed the singing birds, bright sky, and shining sun. He felt all right. Pete then shared the sunglasses with Squirrel, who was mad because she found only one acorn. The glasses helped Squirrel feel happy too. Next, Pete helped Turtle, who was frustrated and upside down, and Alligator, who was sad because no one wanted to play. Each friend looked through the glasses and saw good things around them. Then Pete fell, and the sunglasses broke. Pete worried without them. Wise Old Al told Pete that he did not need magic sunglasses. Pete looked around and saw the good things again. He felt all right and remembered to look for the good in every day.

Pete the cat was grumpy, even though he had never felt grumpy before. Grumpy Toad gave him magic sunglasses that helped him see the world in a new way. When Pete wore them, he saw birds singing, a bright sky, and a shining sun, so he felt better. Pete met Squirrel, Turtle, and Alligator. Squirrel was mad because she found only one acorn. Turtle was frustrated because he was all upside down. Alligator was sad because no one wanted to play. Pete let each friend try the sunglasses. Each animal looked around, noticed the good things, and felt better. Later, Pete fell and the sunglasses broke. He did not know what to do without them. Wise Old Al explained that Pete did not need magic sunglasses to see in a new way. Pete looked around by himself and saw the singing birds, bright sky, and shining sun. He and his friends felt all right.

Pete began his day feeling unhappy and grumpy. Grumpy Toad showed him cool blue magic sunglasses and said they could make the blues go away. Pete wore them and saw that the birds were singing, the sky was bright, and the sun was shining. Then Pete helped his friends. Squirrel felt mad because she had found only one acorn. Turtle felt frustrated because he was upside down. Alligator felt sad because nobody wanted to play. Pete gave each friend the sunglasses, and each one saw the good things around them. Soon Pete fell, and the glasses broke. Pete was unsure what to do. Wise Old Al told him that he could see things in a new way without magic glasses. Pete looked around and saw the birds, sky, and sun. He felt all right again. Pete learned to look for the good in every day, even without the sunglasses.

video_title: MOANA Becoming a Wayfinder | Bedtime Story for Kids

summaries.summary: At sunset, Maui looks at the stars and tastes the ocean. He says they must go east to find Tamatoa, who may have Maui’s hook. Moana is excited because they are going to help the islands. Maui sails the canoe, and Moana watches him carefully. She wants to learn wayfinding, but Maui says she is a princess and cannot be a wayfinder. He puts her in the cargo hold. Then a blow dart paralyzes Maui. Moana helps him onto the outrigger and asks him to teach her. Maui gives her sailing jobs. She pulls the rope, steers the canoe, and works hard when the wind and waves move the boat. Heihei pecks at Maui’s moving tattoo. At last, Moana guides the canoe more easily. She becomes tired, but she keeps saying, “I can do it,” because she wants to prove it to Maui and herself.

Maui and Moana travel east in their canoe as stars appear. Maui uses the stars, the water, the sea, and the wind to find the way to Tamatoa’s lair. Moana wants to learn from him. Maui tells her that wayfinding means seeing where you are going and knowing where you are by knowing where you have been. He says Moana is a princess, not a wayfinder, and places her in the cargo hold. Soon, a blow dart leaves Maui unable to move. Moana brings him onto the outrigger and makes him teach her. She learns to measure the stars, feel the current, untie the right rope, and steer. The wind pulls the rope, and the waves rock the canoe, but Moana keeps working. She guides the boat more smoothly. When she grows sleepy and tired, she repeats, “I can do it,” to show Maui and herself that she can learn.

Moana watches Maui sail toward the east. He says they are going to find Tamatoa, who may have his hook. Moana asks to learn sailing and wayfinding. Maui explains that wayfinding is more than sails and knots, but he says Moana cannot be a wayfinder and puts her in the cargo hold. A blow dart hits Maui, and he becomes paralyzed. Moana helps him and tells him that if he can talk, he can teach. Maui gives her instructions while she steers. She makes mistakes with the stars, the water, the ropes, and the oar. The wind fills the sail, and the canoe moves through choppy waves. Moana pulls the rope back and turns the canoe. Heihei bothers Maui’s tattoo, making Maui shout. Moana keeps trying. She finds the right course and holds the canoe steady, even when she is tired. She says, “I can do it,” again and again.

video_title: Part 2/3 of George's Marvellous Medicine by Roald Dahl. Read-aloud/audiobook with illustrations.

summaries.summary: George gives Grandma a spoonful of his strange brown medicine. It makes her jump into the air, smoke, swell up, shrink, and then grow taller and taller. George gives her another spoonful, and she breaks through the ceilings until her head comes out through the farmhouse roof. George worries that he will be blamed for damaging the house. He tests the medicine on a brown hen. The hen shoots into the air, smokes, performs a somersault, and grows as large as a horse. George's parents see the giant hen and Grandma. Mr. Cranky is excited because he wants enormous farm animals. George gives medicine to the pig, bullocks, sheep, pony, and nanny goat. A crane lifts Grandma down from the roof. The medicine cures her aches, but she remains grumpy and must sleep in the barn. Mr. Cranky decides to make and sell more medicine, but George cannot remember the recipe. They collect empty containers and buy fresh ingredients to try again.

Grandma demands her medicine from George, so he gives her a whole spoonful. The medicine causes a series of amazing changes: Grandma flies from her chair, smokes like she is burning, fills with strange movements, swells, shrinks, and finally grows through the ceilings. She asks George for more, and the second dose sends her head through the roof. George tests the remaining medicine on a brown hen. The hen first flies upward, smokes, and acts sick, but then it does a somersault and grows until it is as big as a horse. George's mother and father arrive. Mr. Cranky is thrilled by the giant hen and gives medicine to the farm animals because he dreams of breeding huge animals. Grandma is lifted from the roof by a crane and rides the giant pony, although she must sleep in the hay barn. The next morning, Mr. Cranky plans a medicine factory, but George admits he cannot remember every ingredient.

George's homemade medicine has a powerful effect on Grandma. After drinking it, she rises into the air, breathes black smoke, feels wild movements in her stomach, and grows so tall that she breaks through the house and roof. She insists that she has magic powers, while George knows that he made the medicine. A brown hen drinks some of the mixture and has similar strange effects. It flies, smokes, jumps like an acrobat, and grows to the size of a horse. George's parents are astonished. His father, Mr. Cranky, sees a chance to create giant pigs, bullocks, sheep, and other animals for farmers. After the animals are dosed, Grandma is removed from the roof with a crane. She feels healthier but is still bad-tempered, so she sleeps in the barn. Mr. Cranky wants to make more medicine and become rich. He asks George to repeat the recipe, but George cannot remember all the things he used. They search the house and shed for empty bottles and buy supplies.

video_title: Super Great Kids' Stories - World Wide Stories for Kids - Mrs Rabbit and the Fox

summaries.summary: Long ago, Mrs. Rabbit, a white rabbit who loved her clean fur, found a little house in a field. She moved in and filled it with tables, chairs, curtains, and a bed. Mrs. Rabbit cleaned all day. First, a little mouse came in, but he ran around looking for cheese. Then a cat came in and chased the mouse. A dog came in and chased the cat, jumping on the clean furniture with muddy paws. Mrs. Rabbit tried to clean, watch the mouse, stop the cat, and push away the dog all at once. Then Mr. Fox arrived. He tricked the mouse, cat, and dog into leaving by promising cheese, fish, and a bone. When they were gone, he moved toward frightened Mrs. Rabbit with his sharp teeth. The animals returned, angry because there were no treats, and chased Mr. Fox away. The house became very dirty, so Mrs. Rabbit returned happily to her burrow.

Mrs. Rabbit loved her beautiful white fur and wanted a little house that she could keep perfectly clean. She moved into a house and spent every day dusting, polishing, brushing, and shining. While she cleaned the windows, a mouse came inside and searched the floor for food. A cat followed and chased the mouse. Then a dog came in and chased the cat, leaving muddy pawprints on the furniture. Mrs. Rabbit tried to manage everyone while still cleaning. Mr. Fox came next. He said he would help by sending the mouse outside for cheese, the cat outside for fish, and the dog outside for a bone. His real plan was to be alone with Mrs. Rabbit. He opened his jaws and came closer, frightening her. Suddenly, the mouse, cat, and dog came back because the promised food was not there. They chased Mr. Fox away. Mrs. Rabbit saw her messy house and chose her burrow instead.

A white rabbit named Mrs. Rabbit believed a house would be a wonderful place to live because she could keep it clean. She bought furniture and cleaned constantly. One day, a mouse visited. The mouse would not stay quietly, so Mrs. Rabbit watched him while washing the windows. A cat then entered and chased the mouse. A dog entered and chased the cat, making the clean house muddy and untidy. Mrs. Rabbit tried to control all three visitors with her paws, head, and hind leg. Mr. Fox came and called the visitors outside by promising each one a favorite food. After they left, he showed his sharp teeth and moved toward Mrs. Rabbit. The mouse, cat, and dog discovered that the cheese, fish, and bone were not real. They returned and chased Mr. Fox out of the house. Mrs. Rabbit saw the dirt and damage. She decided houses were not right for her, and she happily went back to her burrow.

video_title: The Bad Seed. by Jory John and illustrated by Pete Oswald.(The Food Group)Read Aloud Kids Books

summaries.summary: A seed thinks he is a bad seed. He does not put things away, comes late, tells long jokes, cuts in line, stares at people, and does not listen. He says he cannot help it. Long ago, he was a humble seed on a sunflower. He lived with many seeds, and they had fun together. Then the flower drooped, and the seeds were put in a bag. Everything became dark. The seed was almost swallowed by a giant, but he was spit out and landed under bleachers. A wad of gum softened his fall. After that, he stopped smiling and lived alone in a soda can. Later, he decided he did not want to be bad anymore. He began trying to be happy. He still made mistakes, but he also said please and thank you, smiled, and held doors open. He kept trying and felt he might not be so bad after all.

The story is about a seed who calls himself bad. Other seeds say he is bad because he is late, cuts in line, tells jokes without endings, and does not listen. The seed remembers that he was not always this way. He began as a simple seed on a sunflower, surrounded by a big family. Then the sunflower drooped, and the seed ended up in a dark bag. A giant nearly swallowed him, but the seed was spit out. He flew under some bleachers and landed with a thud. Gum helped soften his fall. After this, he changed. He stopped smiling, kept away from everyone, and lived inside a soda can. One day, he made a big decision. He wanted to be happy instead of bad. He still forgot things and talked during movies, but he also used kind words, smiled, and held doors open. He learned to keep trying.

A little seed says, “I’m a bad seed.” He admits that he is rude in many ways. He does not return things, washes neither his hands nor his feet, lies about small things, cuts in line, glares at people, and finishes their sentences. He says he was once a happy, humble seed in a sunflower family. When the flower drooped, the seeds went into a bag. The seed became scared in the dark and was almost swallowed by a giant. At the last moment, he was spit out. He landed under bleachers, where gum softened his fall. Afterward, he became lonely and stopped smiling. He lived in a soda can and did not care. Then he decided to change. Being good was difficult because he was used to being bad, but he tried one day at a time. He began saying please and thank you, smiling, and holding doors. Sometimes he still felt bad, but sometimes he felt good too.

video_title: 🦕 Danny and the Dinosaur School Days 🦕 Stories for Kids Read Aloud [ READ ALONG VIDEO ]

summaries.summary: A dinosaur wondered why dinosaurs did not go to school. He knew that his friend Danny liked school, so he left the museum and followed Danny's yellow bus. At school, Danny and his teacher welcomed him into the class, even though he was a little big for the room. The dinosaur enjoyed learning the ABCs, math, measurements, and about life long ago. The children made dinosaur art and practiced stomping like dinosaurs. After the morning lessons, everyone hurried to lunch. The cafeteria food was sloppy toes, but the dinosaur said it was not dinosaur food. Danny and the dinosaur went outside and ate lunch together. The whole class came out to play on the grass. The dinosaur said school was fun. Danny's teacher said the dinosaur was fun too. The class gave him a present, and he went home while everyone waved and invited him back.

The dinosaur wanted to find out what school was like because Danny always made it sound fun. One day, the dinosaur left the museum and followed Danny's yellow bus. Danny was surprised to see him, but the teacher welcomed him to class. The dinosaur learned ABCs while the children learned math, measurements, and about the time when dinosaurs lived. They made dinosaur pictures and stomped like dinosaurs. Soon the bell rang, and everyone became hungry. At lunchtime, the dinosaur saw that the cafeteria had sloppy toes. He did not think that was dinosaur food, so Danny helped him get a pass to eat outside. Danny and the dinosaur ate their lunches together, and then the entire class played on the grass with them. The dinosaur discovered that school really was fun. The teacher said the dinosaur was fun too. The class gave him a present, and Danny and his friends waved as he went home.

A dinosaur asked himself why dinosaurs did not go to school. Since he knew Danny enjoyed school, he walked away from the museum and followed Danny's bus. At school, Danny introduced him to the teacher. The dinosaur squeezed into the class and joined the lessons. He loved learning his ABCs. The class also studied math, measurements, and what life was like 100 million years ago. The students created dinosaur art and practiced stomping. After a busy morning, the lunch bell rang. The dinosaur followed Danny, but the cafeteria had sloppy toes, which the dinosaur did not want because it was not dinosaur food. Danny and the dinosaur went outside with a pass. They ate lunch, and soon the whole class joined them on the grass. The dinosaur said school was fun, and the teacher agreed that he was fun too. The class gave him a present. Everyone cheered and waved while he headed home, telling him to come back anytime.

video_title: 🐾 Fancy Nancy Time For Puppy School 🐾| Kids Books Read Aloud!

summaries.summary: Fancy Nancy is excited because school will start soon, but she will miss her dog, Frenchie. They played together all summer, and Nancy loves her very much. Frenchie is fun, but she sometimes gets into trouble. She tries to play with Nancy’s belt, jumps on the table, barks for people food, and pulls the fancy ribbons and decorations off Nancy’s new purple backpack. Nancy is upset, but Frenchie looks sorry, so Nancy gives her a kiss. Nancy’s mother says Frenchie should go to puppy school. Frenchie starts on Monday and carries Nancy’s old backpack filled with treats. At school, Frenchie learns how to behave. By the end of the week, she plays with her own toys, stops barking and begging for food, and leaves people’s things alone. Nancy is proud because Frenchie has become a very good student.

Nancy gets ready for school and makes a beautiful new backpack. She chooses a purple one, ties ribbons around it, makes big bows, and adds her name with jewel stickers. Nancy thinks she will learn a great deal at school. Frenchie is nearby, but she does not always behave well. She wants to play with Nancy’s belt and barks at dinner because she wants the family’s food. Later, Nancy discovers that the decorations have been pulled off her backpack. She knows Frenchie did it. Frenchie looks sorry, and Nancy still gives her a kiss because she loves her. Nancy’s mother decides that Frenchie needs puppy school. Frenchie goes to class with an old backpack full of treats. After learning from the teacher, Frenchie uses only her toys, stops begging and barking, and leaves people’s things alone. Nancy is proud of her good puppy.

School is about to begin, and Nancy feels thrilled. She and Frenchie spent the summer together, so Nancy knows she will miss her dog. Nancy prepares a new purple backpack with ribbons, bows, and jewel stickers. Frenchie causes trouble while Nancy gets ready. She tries to tug Nancy’s belt, jumps on the table, barks for dinner, and later removes the decorations from the backpack. Nancy tells Frenchie that she was naughty, but Frenchie looks sorry, and Nancy gives her a big kiss. Nancy’s mother sends Frenchie to puppy school. Frenchie wears Nancy’s old backpack and watches the teacher train the dogs. During the week, Frenchie learns to play with her own toys, stay quiet instead of begging for food, and leave people’s belongings alone. Nancy says Frenchie is the best puppy ever. Before Nancy’s first school day, she kisses Frenchie and tells her she is proud.

video_title: 📖 Kids Book Read Aloud 📖 What If Everybody Did That [ READ ALONG VIDEO ]

summaries.summary: A child keeps doing small things that seem harmless. At the zoo, the child feeds popcorn to a bear. The child makes a grocery cart go fast, drops one soda can from a car, licks frosting at a wedding, and tells the babysitter that baths happen only once a year. The child talks during story time, honks the car horn, splashes at the pool, stands on the bus, leaves a coat on the school floor, throws a snowball, shoots a straw wrapper at dinner, and runs onto a football field. Each time, an adult asks, “What if everybody did that?” At the end, the child comes home and gives Mom a hug. Then the child asks the same question and says, “Everybody should.” The story shows that some actions should not be copied, while kind actions should be shared by everyone.

The child in the story often says, “I just did a little.” A little popcorn is fed to a bear, a grocery cart is pushed too fast, and one soda can is dropped from a car window. At a wedding, the child licks the cake frosting. The child says baths happen once a year, speaks before story time is over, honks the horn, splashes in the pool, and stands on a bus to look at a fire truck. At school, the child leaves a coat down and throws a snowball at Sammy. At dinner, the child shoots a straw wrapper, and after a football game, the child runs onto the field. Zookeepers, managers, patrolmen, librarians, teachers, and other adults all ask what would happen if everyone acted that way. When the child gets home, the child hugs Mom. That is the one action the child says everybody should do.

During many ordinary days, a child makes choices that cause trouble. The child feeds popcorn to a zoo bear, races a grocery cart, throws a can from a car, and licks a fancy cake. The child tells a babysitter about taking a bath only once a year and interrupts story time. The child honks the horn while waiting for Dad, splashes at the swimming pool, and stands up on the bus. At school, the child leaves a coat on the rack area and throws a snowball at Sammy, so the coat must be picked up and the child must stand by the wall. The child also throws a straw wrapper and runs onto a football field for an autograph. Again and again, grown-ups ask, “What if everybody did that?” At home, the child hugs Mom and says everyone should do that. The ending points to sharing kindness, not careless behavior.

video_title: The Rabbit Listened By: Cori Doerrfeld

summaries.summary: Taylor builds something new and special, and feels proud. Suddenly, everything comes crashing down. Several animal friends come to help. The chicken wants Taylor to talk. The bear wants Taylor to shout. The elephant wants Taylor to remember how things were. Other animals want to laugh, hide, throw everything away, or knock down someone else’s towel. Taylor does not feel like doing any of those things, so the animals leave. Taylor is alone and quiet. Then a rabbit comes close and sits beside Taylor. Taylor asks the rabbit to stay. The rabbit listens while Taylor talks, shouts, remembers, and laughs. The rabbit also listens to Taylor’s plans to hide, throw things away, or ruin something for someone else. The rabbit never leaves. When Taylor is ready, the rabbit listens to Taylor’s plan to build again. Taylor says it will be amazing.

One day, Taylor decides to build something special. Taylor is proud of it, but then the things come crashing down. Many animals try to help. The chicken says they should talk about it. The bear says they should shout because Taylor may feel angry. The elephant says they can fix it by remembering the way it was. The hyenas want to laugh, the ostrich wants to hide, the kangaroo wants to throw the mess away, and the snake wants to knock down someone else’s towel. Taylor does not want to talk, shout, remember, laugh, hide, throw things away, or do something with the animals. The animals leave, and Taylor sits alone in the quiet. A rabbit moves close and sits silently with Taylor. Taylor asks the rabbit to stay. The rabbit listens to every feeling and plan. At last, Taylor is ready to build again and says, “It’s gonna be amazing.”

Taylor starts to build something new, special, and amazing. Then it falls down, and Taylor feels unable to talk or do what the animal friends suggest. The chicken suggests talking. The bear suggests shouting. The elephant suggests remembering. The hyenas suggest laughing, the ostrich suggests hiding, the kangaroo suggests throwing away the mess, and the snake suggests knocking down someone else’s towel. Taylor does not want to do anything with anybody, so all the animals leave. Taylor is alone. A rabbit quietly comes closer and sits beside Taylor. Taylor feels the rabbit’s warm body and asks, “Please stay with me.” The rabbit listens while Taylor talks, shouts, remembers, and laughs. It listens to Taylor’s other plans too, without leaving. When Taylor is ready, the rabbit listens to a new plan: build again. Taylor feels excited and says, “I can’t wait. It’s gonna be amazing.”

video_title: 🌞 My Many Colored Days

summaries.summary: Some days are yellow, and some days are blue. On different days, the speaker is different too. On bright red days, being a horse feels good, and the speaker kicks up their heels. On other days, the speaker is other things. On bright blue days, the speaker flops their wings. Some days feel sort of broke, slow, and low-down. Then comes a busy day. On a gray day, everything is great, but the speaker watches while nothing moves. All of a sudden, the speaker is a circus seal. Orange days feel a certain way. Green days are deep in the sea, where the speaker is a quack-quack fish. Purple days are sad and lonely. Pink days are happy, and jumping feels good. Black days are mad and loud. At last comes a mixed-up day. The speaker does not know what or who they are, but everything turns out all right, and they can go back to being themself.

The speaker has many different colored days. Yellow and blue days feel different, and the speaker changes in many ways. On a bright red day, the speaker feels good as a horse and keeps their heels. On a bright blue day, the speaker flops wings. Some days feel broke, slow, and low-down. Then a busy day comes. On a gray day, the speaker watches, but nothing moves. Suddenly, the speaker becomes a circus seal. Orange days show another feeling. Green days are deep in the sea, and the speaker is a quack-quack fish. Purple days are sad. The speaker says they grew up, drank their tail, and walked alone. Pink days are happy days for jumping without thinking. Black days are mad and loud, and the speaker growls at every cloud. Then a mixed-up day arrives. The speaker does not know who or what they are. Still, it turns out all right, and the speaker can go back to being themself.

This story moves through many colored days. The speaker says that different days bring different feelings and different ways of being. Red days feel good, like being a horse and keeping heels. Blue days bring wings that flop. Some days feel broke, slow, and low-down. Then comes a busy day. A gray day is great, even though the speaker watches and nothing moves. Suddenly, the speaker is a circus seal. Orange days have their own feeling. Green days are deep in the sea, where the speaker is a quack-quack fish. Purple days are sad, and the speaker walks alone. Pink days are happy, and the speaker jumps and does not think. Black days are mad and loud, so the speaker growls at clouds. Then comes a mixed-up day, and the speaker does not know who or what they are. In the end, things turn out all right, and the speaker asks if they can go back to being themself.

video_title: 🎄Kids Read Aloud Books : World of Reading : Disney Pinocchio : A Meowy Christmas

summaries.summary: Pinocchio and his father, Jepetto, wake up and eat eggs and bacon. Then they see snow outside and begin getting ready for Christmas. They decorate the workshop, hang stockings, make supper, and decorate the Christmas tree. Figuro the kitten wants to help put the star on the tree, but he cannot reach it. He feels sad. Later, Figuro finds presents under the bed, but there is no present for him. When Pinocchio and Jepetto leave, Figuro becomes angry and ruins the wrapping paper, ornaments, ribbons, and decorations. He is about to eat the Christmas goose when Jiminy Cricket arrives. Jiminy tells Figuro that Christmas is not about gifts or decorations. Together, they fix the workshop. When Pinocchio and Jepetto return, they like the decorations and give Figuro a present. Figuro learns that Christmas is about spending time with family.

Snow falls outside the workshop, so Pinocchio, Jepetto, and Figuro get ready for Christmas. Jepetto places decorations around the room. Pinocchio hangs bows and puts garland around Cleo's fish tank. They hang stockings, cook stuffing, potatoes, and a goose, and place a star on the Christmas tree. Figuro wants to help with the star, but he cannot reach it. He feels unhappy and hides under the bed. There he sees Christmas presents for everyone except himself. Figuro watches Pinocchio and Jepetto leave and becomes mad. He tears the wrapping paper, knocks ornaments from the tree, pulls down ribbons, and removes the decorations. Just before he eats the goose, Jiminy Cricket appears. Jiminy helps Figuro understand that this is not what Christmas is about. They work together to wrap the presents and decorate again. Pinocchio and Jepetto come home, love the new decorations, and give Figuro a gift. Figuro is happy and learns that family time matters most.

Pinocchio is excited when he sees snow outside with his father, Jepetto. Everyone prepares for Christmas. They decorate the workshop, hang stockings, cook a Christmas Eve meal, and put a star on the tree. Figuro the kitten wants to put up the star, but he cannot reach it, so he becomes sad. Under Jepetto's bed, Figuro finds presents for everyone but himself. He thinks Pinocchio and Jepetto are going on a Christmas adventure without him, and he gets angry. Figuro tears the present paper, knocks down tree ornaments, pulls down ribbons, and removes the decorations. He is ready to eat the Christmas goose when Jiminy Cricket stops him. Jiminy says that Christmas is not about gifts or decorations. Figuro feels guilty and helps Jiminy repair everything. They wrap the gifts again and make the workshop look cheerful with candles and red bows. Pinocchio and Jepetto return, give Figuro a present, and make him happy. Figuro learns that Christmas is about spending time with family.

video_title: Jabari Jumps | A Story About Courage, Confidence, and Taking the Leap

summaries.summary: Jabari tells his dad that he will jump from the diving board. He has finished swimming lessons and passed his swim test, so he says he is ready and not scared. He watches other children climb the tall ladder, walk to the edge, and dive into the water. When it is his turn, Jabari waits at the bottom and says he needs to think. He climbs a little, but the ladder feels very tall, and he climbs down for a tiny rest. Jabari remembers that he forgot to stretch and thinks tomorrow may be a better day. His dad tells him it is okay to feel scared and suggests taking a deep breath and saying he is ready. Jabari breathes deeply, climbs to the top, and walks to the edge. He jumps and splashes into the water. He comes back up, and his dad celebrates. Jabari says he is a great jumper, while his dad jokes about a double backflip next.

Jabari is excited to jump off a high diving board. He tells his dad that he is a great jumper, but the board looks high and a little scary. He watches other children jump, and their dives look easy. Jabari reaches the ladder, then lets another child go first while he thinks about a special jump. He climbs upward, but the tall ladder makes him tired, so he rests at the bottom. He also remembers that he forgot his stretches and says maybe he should jump another day. His dad explains that feeling a little scared is okay. He says a deep breath and the words “I am ready” can help the scary feeling become a surprise. Jabari loves surprises. He takes a deep breath, climbs all the way up, and walks to the end of the board. Then he spreads his arms, bends his knees, and flies into the water. After a splash, he comes back up. Jabari is proud because he did it.

At the pool, Jabari wants to make a big jump. He has passed his swim test, but the high diving board makes him feel unsure. He watches children climb, balance at the edge, and dive down with a splash. Jabari waits and says he needs to choose a special jump. He starts up the tall ladder, then decides to take a small rest. At the bottom, he remembers he did not stretch and wonders if he should try tomorrow. His dad tells him that being a little scared is okay. His dad teaches him to take a deep breath and tell himself he is ready. Jabari breathes from his hair to his toes and begins again. He climbs to the top, walks to the rough edge, and looks out. Feeling ready, he takes another breath, spreads his arms, bends his knees, and springs from the board. He splashes into the water and rises again. His dad says he did it, and Jabari proudly agrees. Then his dad mentions a surprise double backflip.

video_title: All Are Welcome – 🏫 Read aloud kids book about diversity and going to school!

summaries.summary: A school day begins with sharpened pencils and ringing bells. The children hurry in because school is beginning and there are dreams to chase. Everyone is welcome, no matter how they start the day, what they wear, when they play, or where they come from. In the classroom, children feel safe, lose their fears, find hope, and take turns speaking. They play music, make art, and share stories. At lunchtime, they pass around many kinds of bread so everyone can eat. After lunch, they swing, slide, and have fun together. The children are part of a community, and their differences make them strong. They learn from one another and discover special talents and a big world. When the busy day ends, they go home to rest and come back ready for a new day. Everyone has a place and is welcome.

The story follows children through a welcoming school day. First, their pencils are ready and the bells ring. They come to school to learn and dream. The classroom welcomes every child, whether the child comes from far away, wears different clothes, plays at a different time, or starts the day in a different way. Inside, the classroom is safe and sound. Children raise their hands and go around together. Then they play music, make art, and share stories from the heart. At lunch, there is a big spread with many kinds of bread, and the children pass food around until everyone is fed. Outside, they swing and slide side by side. They are a community with strength in diversity. They learn from each other and find special talents. At the end, they go home to rest, ready to return tomorrow. The classroom says everyone has a place and is welcome.

The school day starts when bells ring, pencils are sharpened, and children make haste. At this school, all are welcome. It does not matter how a child starts the day, what the child wears, when the child plays, or where the child comes from. In the classroom, everyone is safe. Fears are lost, hope is found, and children raise their hands to take turns. They gather to play music, make art, and share stories. Then they eat lunch together. There are a dozen kinds of bread, and the food is passed around until everyone is fed. After lunch, the doors open and the children swing, slide, and have fun side by side. They belong to a community, and diversity makes the community strong. They learn from each other and discover special talents. When the busy day is over, they go home to rest, greet tomorrow fresh, and come back again. Everyone has a place there.

video_title: Read Aloud Books For Kids | Monty The Manatee | Story About Kindness and Anti-Bullying |Read For Fun

summaries.summary: Monty the manatee felt shy on his first day at Sea school. He waved goodbye to his caring mommy and slowly paddled into school. Monty asked some jellyfish to play, but they told him to leave. Sydney the shrimp called him a wimp, and Sammy Seal did not want his friendship or food. A school of fish also teased Monty and said he was ugly, slow, and clumsy. Then a huge shark came toward all the sea creatures, ready to eat them. Clever Monty closed his eyes and looked like a rock. He tucked his friends under his tummy and stayed still. The shark swam away because he thought Monty was a rock. The sea creatures cheered for Monty and felt sorry for being unkind. They became friends and played nicely. Monty said that what is inside matters more than being fast, slow, thin, or fat, and that kindness makes the world better.

On his first day at Sea school, Monty the manatee wanted a friend. He spoke politely to the jellyfish, but they would not let him join their private chat. Sydney the shrimp called Monty a wimp. At lunch, Sammy Seal refused Monty's food and friendship. Some fish joined the teasing and called Monty the ugliest creature in the sea. Then everyone saw a big shark racing toward them. Monty thought of a plan. He closed his eyes so he would look like a rock, then he placed his friends safely under his tummy. All the animals stayed very still while the shark came near. The shark believed Monty was a rock and moved away. Monty's friends cheered and were sorry they had treated him badly. Monty agreed that they should all be friends. After that, the sea creatures played together nicely. Monty reminded everyone that people can be different on the outside, but what is inside really matters, and unkind words can hurt.

Monty was a shy manatee going to Sea school for the first time. His mommy encouraged him, so he slowly swam inside. Monty tried to make friends with jellyfish, Sydney the shrimp, Sammy Seal, and a school of fish. Each group rejected him or teased him because they thought he was slow, clumsy, or not cool. Suddenly, a huge shark appeared and rushed at the sea creatures. Monty used his clever idea to help them. He closed his eyes and looked like a rock. Then he tucked the others beneath his tummy, and everyone held their breath. The shark came close but thought Monty was only a rock, so the animals were safe. Monty's school friends cheered and apologized for bullying him. Monty wanted the bullying to stop, and he agreed that they could all be friends. From that day, the creatures played nicely. Monty's message was that being slower, faster, thinner, or fatter does not matter as much as what is on the inside, and everyone should be kind.

video_title: 🎄Duck & Goose: It's time for Christmas

summaries.summary: Goose hears that it is not time for catching snowflakes. It is not time for sledding, making snow angels, throwing snowballs, making a snow goose, skating, or building forts. Goose hears the same message again and again as each snowy activity is named. Then someone says, “Come on, Goose.” The message changes. It is time for Christmas. The story moves from many winter activities that are not happening now to Christmas time. Goose is told to leave the snow activities and come along. First, the snow activities are named. Next, Goose hears that none of them is the right time. At the end, the right time is named: it is time for Christmas.

The story talks to Goose about what time it is. First, Goose is told that it is not time for catching snowflakes. It is also not time for sledding or making snow angels. Then it is not time for throwing snowballs, making a snow goose, skating, or building forts. The winter activities come one after another, but none of them is the activity for this moment. After the list, someone says, “Come on, Goose.” Goose is called to come along. Then the final message is given: it is time for Christmas. The story begins with snow play that is not happening now. It continues with more snow play that is not happening now. It ends by saying that Christmas time has come.

Goose is told that several snowy things must wait. Goose cannot catch snowflakes now. Goose cannot sled, make snow angels, throw snowballs, make a snow goose, skate, or build forts now. Each activity is named with the words, “It is not time.” After all the winter activities are listed, someone tells Goose, “Come on.” This means Goose should come along. Then Goose hears the important ending: “It is time for Christmas.” The story has a simple change from “not time” to “time.” At the beginning and middle, Goose hears about snow activities that are not for now. At the end, the waiting is over for the named moment, because Christmas is the time. The story finishes with Goose being called to Christmas time.

video_title: Danger at the Dieselworks {Thomas & Friends} | Kids & Family Picture Story Book Time | Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Thomas and Percy see smoke and hurry to a burning farm shed. They help the farm workers use water, and Belle helps put out the flames. Belle says Sodor needs Flynn, a real fire engine, and Flynn comes. Thomas takes Belle around Sodor, so Percy feels lonely. Diesel invites Percy to the Diesel Works. Percy learns that the Diesels need a crane and thinks he can help. He goes there with Kevin. The Diesels trick Percy into leading them to the Steamworks. They take it, and Thomas is held at the Diesel Works. Percy feels sorry because he made a mistake. Sparks from Percy start another fire. Percy finds Flynn, who saves Thomas and puts out the fire. Sir Topham Hat tells Diesel 10 to be fair and wait. The Diesels and steamies build a new Diesel Works together. Thomas and Percy become happy friends again.

A fire starts at an old farm shed on Sodor. Thomas and Percy help, and Belle uses her water tanks to stop the flames. Belle says Flynn can be a hero, so Flynn arrives. Thomas takes Belle on a tour, and Percy feels left out. Diesel asks Percy to visit the Diesel Works. Percy sees that the Diesels have no crane and wants to tell Sir Topham Hat. Kevin likes being called a hero, so Percy and Kevin stay at the Diesel Works overnight. Then Diesel 10 asks Percy to lead the Diesels to the Steamworks. The Diesels take the Steamworks and say Thomas is a prisoner. Percy understands that this was a bad choice. When he goes back, sparks start a fire. Percy brings Flynn, and Flynn pumps water until the fire goes out. Sir Topham Hat says stealing and trickery are wrong. Everyone works together to make a new Diesel Works.

The day begins calmly, but Thomas and Percy find a fire. Belle helps save the farm shed, and everyone sees that she is useful. Flynn comes to help Sodor too. Percy is sad when Thomas spends time with Belle, so Diesel takes him to the Diesel Works. Percy sees the dark place needs a crane. He hopes Thomas can help, but Diesel 10 has another plan. The Diesels persuade Percy to lead them to the Steamworks. They take it, while Thomas stays at the Diesel Works. Percy knows he has made a terrible mistake. He returns and accidentally makes a fire with sparks from his wheels. Flynn comes with Percy and saves Thomas. Flynn puts out the flames, and Thomas thanks him for being a hero. Sir Topham Hat arrives and explains that the Diesels will get a new building, but they must wait and be fair. The engines build it together, and Thomas and Percy are friends again.

video_title: This Very Tree-A Story of 9/11, Resilience, and Regrowth | Kids Reading Aloud Picture Story Book

summaries.summary: A tree grew in a busy New York City plaza beneath two tall towers. It gave people shade, offered birds a resting place, and blossomed early each spring. One morning, something terrible happened, and the tree was left alone in darkness for weeks. When people found it, the city sounded and smelled different, so they carried the tree to a quiet nursery in a park. The tree was weak, but the workers cared for it through winter, and its leaves returned. Other trees and visiting birds helped it feel stronger. After many years, it was ready to go home. It returned to a new plaza with many trees and three empty spaces. Two spaces marked where the towers had stood, and the third was for the tree. Now its shade gives peace, and its healed branches give hope. Its blossoms still announce that spring will come.

The narrator is a city tree planted in a plaza under two famous towers. Its leaves shade people, its branches shelter birds, and its flowers show that spring has arrived. Then an ordinary morning changed, and the tree remained buried in darkness for weeks. After it was rescued, unfamiliar city noises and smells frightened it. People took it to a nursery in a distant park, where they cared for it all winter. No one knew whether its leaves would return, but they did. A dove nested in its branches, and the tree slowly regrew. Surrounded by other trees, it became strong enough to do its old job again. It traveled back downtown and found a new plaza, a forest of trees, and three saved spaces. Two stayed empty where the towers had been. The tree filled the third space and now helps hurt people find peace and hope.

In New York City, a tree enjoyed life in a busy plaza. It liked the wind between the buildings, the smell of summer rain on concrete, and watching people come and go. Its branches held birds, and its early flowers told everyone that spring was near. Then the tree experienced a disaster and spent weeks alone in darkness. Afterward, people moved it to a quiet park nursery. The tree had changed, but careful workers protected it through winter, and new leaves grew. Birds returned, including a dove that built a nest. As years passed, the tree became stronger and decided it was ready to return home. Downtown, it saw a shining spire, new towers, and a forest planted in a new plaza. Two empty places honored the former towers, while a third held the tree. Its healed branches now offer peace and hope, and its blossoms continue to promise spring.

video_title: Thumbelina | A Classic English Fairy Tale | Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: Long ago, a farmer found a big pea pod in his garden. When it opened, a tiny girl was inside. She was as big as the farmer’s thumb, so the farmer and his wife named her Thumbelina. She played on the kitchen table and slept in a walnut-shell bed. One day, a big toad carried Thumbelina away to a water lily because he wanted to marry her. Thumbelina did not want to live with the toad, so she cried and asked two little fish for help. The fish bit through the leaf’s stalk, and Thumbelina floated away. Her leaf reached a rock, where she met a little blue bird. She asked the bird to help her go home. The bird carried her over the river and fields. At last, Thumbelina reached the farmer’s house and was very happy to be home again.

A farmer discovered a tiny girl inside a pea pod. She was no bigger than his thumb, so he and his wife called her Thumbelina. Thumbelina lived happily with them. She played on the kitchen table and slept at night in a bed made from a walnut shell. Then a large toad came from the river. He saw Thumbelina and carried her to a water lily because he wanted to marry her. Thumbelina was unhappy and wanted to go home. Two fish heard her crying. When she asked for help, they used their sharp teeth to bite through the leaf stalk. The leaf broke free and carried Thumbelina away. Soon, she came to a rock and saw a little blue bird. The bird told her to climb on its back. It flew across the river and fields, taking Thumbelina back to the farmer’s house, where she was happy again.

Thumbelina began life in a big pea pod found by a farmer. The pod opened the next morning, and a tiny girl appeared. Because she was as big as the farmer’s thumb, the farmer and his wife gave her the name Thumbelina. She enjoyed playing on the kitchen table and slept in a walnut shell. One night, a toad carried her from the house to a water lily on the river. The toad wanted to marry her, but Thumbelina did not want to stay with him. She cried and asked two nearby fish to help her return home. The fish bit the stalk holding the leaf, and Thumbelina floated away. Her leaf reached a rock, where she found a little blue bird. She asked for help, and the bird let her climb onto its back. The bird flew over the river and fields and brought Thumbelina back to the farmer’s house. She was very happy to be home.

video_title: MOANA The Story of a New Home | Bedtime Story for Kids

summaries.summary: A group of men, women, and children sailed west for three months. They used the Sun in the day and the stars at night to find their way. Their master wayfinder, Matai Vasa, watched the wind, waves, clouds, and sky. One day, he saw a dark patch beneath the clouds. He guided the canoes to a green island surrounded by a reef. The canoes entered a calm lagoon, and everyone stepped onto the shore. Seeds from Matai Vasa's clothing grew into a wide banyan tree. The people built a village, planted crops, gathered forest fruit, and fished in the lagoon. They named their home Montanui. They still loved the sea. Young wayfinders learned from their mentors, and Mataivasa taught his protégé. Later, the protégé sailed beyond the reef with a crew. The villagers watched, knowing the winds would carry them home.

Matai Vasa led his people across the water to find a new home. They sailed by the Sun and stars, carrying children, animals, seeds, and tools. On the third day, Matai Vasa saw a small dark place under some clouds. He knew it was an island and steered the people toward it. The island had tall green peaks and a coral reef around it. The reef protected a quiet lagoon, so the canoes could pass safely between the rocks and beach. The people came ashore with happy faces. Seeds fell from Matai Vasa's clothing and grew into a banyan tree with wide branches and deep roots. The tribe also grew. They made a village, planted fields, picked fruit, and fished. Their home was called Montanui. Later, young wayfinders learned about weather, stars, and currents. Matai Vasa gave his shell necklace to his protégé, who sailed away and would return home.

The travelers came from the West and sailed toward an island they believed was waiting for them. For three months, they followed the Sun by day and the stars by night. Matai Vasa was their master wayfinder. He listened to the sea and watched the clouds and wind. On the third day, he noticed a darker patch beneath the clouds and guided the people toward it. They found a green island surrounded by coral. The reef protected a peaceful lagoon, and the canoes moved through it to the beach. The people began a new life there. Seeds became a banyan tree, and the tribe built a village called Montanui. They cleared fields, gathered fruit, and fished. Still, the people heard the sea calling. Young wayfinders studied with mentors. Mataivasa taught his protégé everything he knew, then gave him the shell necklace. The protégé sailed beyond the reef, while the villagers watched with excitement.

video_title: Clifford's Birthday Party - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

summaries.summary: Emily Elizabeth plans a birthday party for her dog, Clifford. She invites his friends and makes ice cream, cookies, and decorations. When the party starts, the friends are not there. Emily finds them at the playground. They are worried because they do not have good presents for Clifford. Emily tells them Clifford will like anything they bring. The friends go home and return with gifts. Scott brings a big ball, and Clifford makes it bigger. Sam brings a pinata with treats for the dogs. Jenny brings a small toy that fits Clifford’s nose. Alicia and Nero bring a talking toy dog. Cynthia brings a gift certificate for a dog haircut. Clifford’s friends enjoy the party. Then Clifford’s family comes out for the cake. Clifford likes his gifts, but being with his family and friends is the best birthday present of all.

Clifford is having a birthday party with Emily Elizabeth. His friends are invited, and Emily prepares cookies, ice cream, and decorations. But nobody comes when the party begins. Emily and Clifford look for the friends and find them together at the playground. Jenny explains that they want to come, but they think their presents are not good enough for Clifford. Emily says Clifford will like whatever they give him. The friends bring their gifts. Clifford plays with a big ball, breaks a pinata, and enjoys a toy that fits his nose. A talking toy dog surprises him when he tries to pet it. Cynthia brings a gift certificate for a shampoo and haircut, but Emily likes Clifford just as he is. At the end, Clifford’s family comes out for the cake. Clifford is happy with his friends and family. Their being together is the best birthday present.

Emily Elizabeth tells about Clifford’s birthday. She invites Clifford’s friends to a party and prepares food and decorations. The friends do not arrive at first, so Emily finds them at the playground. They are staying away because they do not have presents they think are good enough. Emily tells them that Clifford will like their gifts. Everyone comes to the party. Scott brings a ball that Clifford blows up even more. Sam brings a pinata, and the dogs eat the treats inside. Jenny brings a little gift that is just right for Clifford’s nose. Alicia and Nero bring a talking toy dog. Cynthia brings a beauty-parlor certificate, but Emily likes Clifford the way he is. Then everyone eats cake. Clifford is surprised when his mother, father, sisters, and brother appear. He is glad to have the presents, but he is happiest to have his friends and family with him.

video_title: Up in the Garden, Down in the dirt - Narration - NRYKB

summaries.summary: A child and Nana care for a garden through the seasons. In spring, the snow melts, but the dirt must dry and warm before planting. The child and Nana clear old plants, spread compost, plant seeds, and give them water. Under the soil, earthworms, pill bugs, and other tiny creatures dig, chew, and help make the dirt busy. Soon carrots, peas, cucumbers, zucchini, pumpkins, and sunflowers grow. Bees visit flowers, and the child eats a warm tomato. Many animals find food in the garden and dirt. At night, bats and skunks work while the child sleeps. When autumn comes, the garden turns cool. The child and Nana harvest food for themselves and their neighbors. Frost arrives, and the insects hide under winter blankets. The garden looks quiet, but seeds, insects, and summer days rest below the dirt, waiting for sunshine and new sprouts.

The story looks at a garden above the ground and the busy dirt below it. A child wants to plant seeds, but Nana explains that spring dirt must become warm and dry first. Together, they clean the garden and add compost. Pill bugs eat old leaves and curl into tiny armored balls. When planting time comes, the child makes rows, places seeds, and waters them. Plants grow, flowers bloom, and honeybees carry pollen. Rain fills the soil, and roots drink the water. The garden becomes a place where many creatures eat: ladybugs eat aphids, a robin finds bugs, bats fly over flowers, and skunks dig at night. In autumn, pumpkins turn orange and the family gathers food for neighbors. Frost covers the leaves, so the people spread winter blankets. Ants, beetles, worms, and other creatures hide below. The garden sleeps until warm weather returns.

A child watches Nana work in their garden from spring until winter. At first, old snow covers the ground, and Nana says it is too early to plant. The child learns that the dirt is full of earthworms and insects that dig and stir the soil. They clear weeds, spread compost, and plant seeds in rows. The seeds grow into carrots, peas, cucumbers, zucchini, pumpkins, and sunflowers. Rain reaches the roots, while insects and animals live and feed in the garden. The child enjoys a ripe tomato, and Nana picks green beans. During summer nights, bats swoop, skunks search for cutworms, and a garter snake eats supper. In fall, the family harvests quickly because cold weather is coming. They have enough food for their neighbors. Frost arrives, and tiny creatures curl up or go home underground. The garden becomes quiet, but a new garden is sleeping in the dirt.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: The Story of Snow By Mark Cassino with John Nelson, Ph.D.

summaries.summary: Snow begins high in a very cold cloud. A tiny speck, such as ash, pollen, salt, soil, or bacteria, becomes the center of a snow crystal. Water vapor sticks to the speck, makes a droplet, and freezes into ice. More vapor makes the ice grow into a six-sided crystal with branches and arms. As it falls, the crystal keeps growing, and the cloud’s moisture and temperature help decide its shape. Some crystals become six-armed stars, some become thin plates, and some become pencil-shaped columns. Water molecules make six the special number in snow crystals. Crystals may grow unevenly, become twins, or get bumps. Many crystals can join to make one snowflake. After landing, a crystal quickly stops growing and begins to wither, so it must be caught quickly to see its shape. Snow crystals are usually different, but they share many things, just like people.

In a cold cloud, snow starts with a tiny speck floating in the air. Water vapor sticks to the speck, freezes, and forms a small ice ball. Then the ice grows into a beautiful crystal with six sides and sometimes six branches. While falling through the cloud, the crystal changes according to the cloud’s temperature and moisture. It may become a star-shaped dendrite, a thin hexagonal plate, or a pencil-like column. Water molecules join in groups of six, which explains why snow crystals often have six arms or six sides. Snow crystals are not always perfect. Water droplets can make one arm longer, two crystals can grow together to make a twin, and droplets can freeze onto a crystal to make bumps. When crystals stick together, they form snowflakes. After a crystal lands, it cannot keep growing and soon becomes rounded. Catching one quickly reveals its delicate structure.

A snow crystal grows inside a very cold cloud around a tiny piece of dirt, ash, salt, pollen, soil, or even a living bacterium. Water vapor gathers on this speck and freezes. The crystal grows larger as more vapor attaches to it, and six branches can sprout from its corners. Different cloud conditions create different shapes. Stars have six arms, plates have six straight sides, and columns look like tiny pencils. The six-sided pattern comes from the way water molecules join together. During the fall, crystals can change, break, grow unevenly, join with another crystal, or collect frozen water droplets. Many crystals joined together make a snowflake. A crystal that lands on the ground quickly starts to wither because it is no longer surrounded by the vapor it needs. Its arms break down and become rounded. Snow crystals may look alike, but complicated ones are usually different, like leaves, flowers, and people.

video_title: Bedtime Stories  The Best Bike Ride Ever

summaries.summary: Bonnie O'Boy asks for a bike again and again for one whole week. On the eighth day, her mother and father give her one. Bonnie is very happy and thanks her mother, father, and Charlie. She asks if she may ride. Her father says she must learn how to stop first, but Bonnie has already started going downhill. She rides over bridges, mountains, and elephants. She rides through downpours and windstorms and past a giraffe and giant cheese. She still cannot stop. The ride is thrilling, breathtaking, and dangerous. Then Bonnie sees a truck and stops with a scraped knee. Her mother puts a band-aid on her boo-boo and says she loves her. Her father gives her a bike lesson. Afterward, Bonnie rides often, stopping to smell the roses. Then she wishes for a pony.

For a full week, Bonnie O'Boy says, “I want a bike.” At last, she gets a bike and says, “Oh boy!” She thanks her mother, father, and Charlie. Bonnie asks to ride, but her father tells her that she needs to know how to stop. Before the lesson can begin, Bonnie rides willy-nilly down the hill. She travels over bridges, mountains, and elephants. She goes through downpours and windstorms and past a giraffe. She goes past the giant cheese and into the land of the lost, but she cannot stop. Not stopping feels thrilling and breathtaking, but it is also dangerous. Bonnie sees a truck and finally stops, though she has a scraped knee. Her mother comforts her with a band-aid and loving words. Her father teaches her about the brakes. Then Bonnie rides more carefully and secretly wishes for a pony.

Bonnie O'Boy really wants a bicycle, and she repeats the request for seven days. On the eighth day, she receives a bike and celebrates by saying, “Oh boy!” She asks to ride right away. Her father explains that she must first learn to stop, but Bonnie has already gone down the hill. She rides far and fast over bridges, mountains, and elephants. She rides through rainstorms and windstorms and passes a giraffe and a giant cheese. Bonnie tries hard, but the bike will not stop. The ride is exciting, breathtaking, and dangerous. When a truck appears, Bonnie stops, but she has a scraped knee. Her mother puts a band-aid on her boo-boo and tells her she loves her. Her father gives her a proper bike lesson. Later, Bonnie practices stopping and secretly wishes for a pony.

video_title: 🍜 Magic Ramen: The Story of Momofuku Ando

summaries.summary: After World War II, Ando walked through the damaged streets of Osaka and saw hungry people waiting in the cold for expensive bowls of ramen. He could not forget them. He decided to spend his life making food so people would have enough to eat. After several businesses, Ando lost his money and began dreaming of noodles that families could make quickly and affordably. He mixed flour, salt, water, eggs, powdered milk, and spinach, but many batches failed. He kept trying until he found the right balance. Then he worked to make noodles that could become soup with hot water. One night, he watched Masako fry tempura and noticed the tiny holes in the crispy batter. Ando fried his noodles, added hot water, and discovered that they became soft, tasty ramen in two minutes. His family helped demonstrate the invention. Soon, many kinds of people enjoyed the nutritious, convenient noodles. Ando said that peace follows from a full stomach.

Ando saw a long line of cold, hungry people waiting for ramen in Osaka. The war had made food scarce, and many people had little to eat. Ando believed the world could be peaceful when everyone had enough food, so he chose food as his life's work. Years later, after losing his money in a business deal, he began creating a new ramen. He wanted whole families to make it without waiting, paying high prices, or using an empty stove for a long time. Ando tried many ingredients and methods. Some noodles were crumbly, sticky, brittle, soft, soggy, or too tough. Then he watched Masako cook tempura. The hot oil left tiny holes in the crispy coating. Ando fried noodles in the same way. When he added hot water, the water entered the holes and softened the noodles. In two minutes, the noodles were tender and chewy in hot soup. Ando had invented instant ramen, and people everywhere began eating it.

The story begins when Ando notices people standing for hours in the cold to buy a small bowl of ramen. Osaka is still damaged after the war, and food is scarce. Ando wants to help hungry people, so he makes food his life's work. He starts businesses and thinks about the hungry line for more than ten years. When one business fails, he uses his time to invent better ramen. He mixes many ingredients, including flour, salt, water, eggs, powdered milk, and spinach, but the noodles do not turn out well at first. He keeps experimenting and finds a good balance. He also tries to make noodles that become soup with hot water. At last, Masako's tempura gives him an idea. Frying creates tiny holes in the noodles, allowing hot water to soften them quickly. Ando and his family show customers the new food. Everyone is amazed by the “magic ramen.” It is tasty, nutritious, and easy to make, and Ando connects full stomachs with peace.

video_title: Creepy Carrots! Read Aloud 🥕 | Funny & Spooky Storytime for Kids [English] 2025

summaries.summary: Jasper Rabbit loved eating the fat, crisp carrots from Krakenhopper Field. He took carrots to school, to little league, and home at night. Then he began to hear carrots creeping behind him. He saw strange things while brushing his teeth and felt scared when he came home. His mother said creepy carrots were not real. His father searched the bedroom, but he could not find any carrots. During the week, Jasper kept seeing creepy carrots everywhere. He believed the carrots were real and were coming for him. Jasper made a plan to keep them away. On Saturday, he took supplies to Krakenhopper Field. When the sun went down, he went home and saw no carrot-shaped shadows. Jasper’s plan had worked. No carrots could leave the patch. The carrots cheered because their own plan had worked too. Jasper would never get into their carrot patch again.

Jasper Rabbit could not get enough of the carrots growing in Krakenhopper Field. He pulled them out for snacks on his way to school, practice, and home. After a big game, he heard a soft, sinister sound and thought the carrots were creeping. Soon, he noticed them at home too. His mother said there were no creepy carrots. His father looked under the bed, in the closet, and in the dresser, but he found nothing. Jasper still felt sure that the carrots were real. By the end of the week, he saw creepy carrots creeping everywhere. He decided that the carrots could not trouble him if they could not get out of the field. On Saturday, Jasper gathered supplies and went to Krakenhopper Field. Later, he smiled on his way home because there were no strange shadows. His plan had worked. The carrots cheered because Jasper could never enter their patch again.

Jasper Rabbit loved the carrots in Krakenhopper Field because they were fat, crisp, and free. He ate them often. One day, after a game, Jasper heard something creeping. He looked around, but he saw nothing. That night and on other nights, he became frightened by what he thought were creepy carrots. His mother said they were not real. His father searched the room and told him to sleep, but Jasper stayed scared. Soon, he believed the carrots were coming for him. Then Jasper made a plan. He took supplies to the carrot field on Saturday. When evening came, he went home and found no creepy carrots and no carrot-shaped shadows. Jasper knew his plan had worked because the carrots could not get out of their patch. The carrots were happy too. Their plan had worked, because Jasper would never get into the carrot patch again.

video_title: READ ALOUD of Oh, The Thinks You Can Think by Dr. Seuss -- Books for Kids Read Aloud!

summaries.summary: The story invites children to think about many wonderful things. A child can imagine birds, a horse, and colors such as yellow, blue, red, and pink. If the child tries, they can imagine a Guff going by and funny schlop with a cherry on top. They can think about gloves and snubs, Kitty O Sullivan Krauss in a balloon swimming pool, black water, a white sky, and a boat. They can imagine night, when the birds sleep and three moons are up, and day, when the water is blue and the birds are awake. They can wonder how much water fifty-five elephants drink and how long a zong’s tail is. They can ask about a rink Rinker and a jaibu. They can think of Peter the postman, races, light, bright stairs, ships, and long trips. At the end, they think left, right, low, and high, because many things can be imagined if they try.

A child is told that thinking can make many pictures and questions. First come birds, colors, a horse, and all the things the child can think of. Trying makes it possible to imagine a Guff, wonderful schlop with a cherry, gloves, snubs, and Kitty O Sullivan Krauss in a balloon swimming pool above her house. The child can imagine black water, a white sky, a boat, and bles blowing by. Night has sleeping birds and three moons, while day has blue water and awake birds. The child can wonder about the water drunk by fifty-five elephants and the tail of a zong. More strange thoughts include a rink Rinker’s tooth and meeting a jaibu. Peter the postman crosses the ice every day and twice on Saturdays. The child may imagine races, light, bright stairs, a ship, and a long trip. Finally, the child thinks about left, right, low, and high, if only they try.

The story shows a big world of pretend thoughts. A thinker may picture birds, a horse, and many bright colors, then imagine a Guff going by. There is no need to stop, because the thinker can make up schlop with a cherry on top, gloves, snubs, and a balloon swimming pool over Kitty O Sullivan Krauss’s house. The thinker can picture black water, a white sky, and a boat blowing by. They can imagine a quiet night with sleeping birds and three moons, or a blue day with birds awake. They can wonder how much water fifty-five elephants drink and how long a zong’s tail is. They can wonder about a rink Rinker’s tooth and a jaibu. Peter the postman crosses the ice once each day and twice on Saturdays. Then come thoughts of races, light, bright stairs, a ship, and a long trip. The story ends by inviting thoughts of left, right, low, and high.
